5. ECO: public registry and trusted publishing; phase 1 ships a signed first-party package index, STEP AP242 (geometry, structure, semantic PMI write), AP203 and AP214 read, and 3MF with beam lattice.
6. AGT: Bayesian exploration, hosted crew, quarantined extraction, TypeScript SDK; phase 1 ships `api` over MCP, Rust and Python SDKs, Propose with CI report, risk classes and two roles (detail designer, verifier).
7. FLX: guaranteed equilibrated estimators on cut cells (FLX open question 11), GPU sign-off paths, CubeCL; phase 1 ships one immersed discretization (shifted boundary interactive, CutFEM sign-off), DWR, p-multigrid with an AMG coarse level, steady adjoints and density topology optimization.
8. ANV: SubD, certified SSI for general NURBS–NURBS pairs, free-form offsets, healing beyond the CAx-IF corpus; phase 1 certifies SSI among planes, quadrics, tori, extrusion and revolution surfaces, and NURBS–analytic pairs.
9. PLT: TUF delta updates (full signed packages suffice), the MSI wrapper, Flatpak, AppImage, reproducible builds beyond Linux and wasm32, telemetry, enterprise policy; phase 1 ships MSIX, a notarized DMG, deb and rpm.
10. ELX: no team before the phase 1 gate beyond a two-person circuit-simulation research track.

**Problem:** No tab sequences work across tabs, yet phase 1 has two long chains and one coupling point. **Section:** CONTRACT §13 Roadmap and golden products (GP1, GP2); MFG Phasing
**Problem:** MFG reads the GP1 gate as "programs pass every oracle and are cut at the reference shop", which puts Crucible's own CAM (2.5D and 3-axis strategies, adaptive clearing after a freedom-to-operate review, two posts, stock and collision simulation) and its own slicer on the phase 1 critical path. That is roughly 20 to 25 EY (estimate) of work that the code-CAD and printing wedge does not need to prove.

**Fix:** Replace the gate texts: "GP1: designed, toleranced, simulated and released in Crucible; manufactured by a reference shop from Crucible's STEP AP242 with semantic PMI and drawing, using the shop's own CAM; measured by external metrology against Crucible's tolerances. GP2: optimized and verified in Crucible; printed from Crucible's 3MF with the printer vendor's slicer; measured externally." **Section:** CONTRACT §9 Platforms; PLT Platform matrix, Tier 1
**Problem:** All eight Tier 1 targets must ship the full product at phase 1 with every golden product passing. For Windows ARM64, Linux ARM64, Safari and Firefox the platform risks (R6-12, R6-31, browser GPU availability) make simultaneous general availability the largest schedule risk, and cutting features on those targets would break the identical-features requirement.
**Evidence:** Chrome on Windows ARM64 enables WebGPU only with `--enable-unsafe-webgpu`, and Firefox ships WebGPU on Linux in Nightly only (gpuweb Implementation Status). Wasmtime rates `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` Tier 3 (docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-tiers). The crash-handling crates list no Windows aarch64 support (github.com/EmbarkStudios/crash-handling).
**Fix:** Add to §9: "A Tier 1 target may be designated Tier 1 preview for at most one phase. A preview target runs the same build with identical features, passes the determinism suite and the golden-product checks headless, and ships through the beta channel; installers, updater, accessibility certification and GPU-driver qualification complete by the next gate." Phase 1 general availability: Windows 11 x86-64, macOS, Linux x86-64, Chrome and Edge. Tier 1 preview in phase 1, general availability at the phase 2 gate: Windows 11 ARM64, Linux ARM64, Safari, Firefox.

**Section:** CONTRACT §13 (no targets); PLT Performance engineering, Reference hardware and Budgets (D-PLT-28)
**Problem:** Contract v3 holds no performance targets and no reference machine, yet ANV, FLX, ING, KLN, MEC and UIX cite "the contract's" 2 s rebuild, 100 ms preview, 1 s simulation update, 10 s assembly and 60 fps rows. PLT's rows come "from the overview", and D-PLT-28 binds every OS's mid machine to an unnamed laptop whose two x86 candidates differ about 2× in hardware threads, differ in ISA level, and differ in browser GPU path under Linux.
**Evidence:** 00-contract.md contains no millisecond, frame-rate or reference-laptop figure. Core Ultra 7 258V: 8 cores, 8 threads, "Intel SSE4.1, Intel SSE4.2, Intel AVX2", Arc 140V (Intel ARK). Ryzen AI 9 HX 370: 12 cores, 24 threads, AVX-512 listed (amd.com). Chrome ships WebGPU on Linux for "Intel Gen12+" and "NVIDIA (driver 535.183.01+) Wayland" only; other GPUs are "Behind a flag" (gpuweb Implementation Status), so the AMD candidate runs browsers on WebGL2 under Linux.
**Fix:** Add contract §13.2 "Performance targets", owned by PLT, holding the core rows as corrected in R6-08 to R6-11. Fix the reference now: Core Ultra 7 258V, 32 GB, Windows 11 and Ubuntu LTS dual boot, measured at 1920×1080 render resolution. It is the weaker candidate (no AVX-512, 8 threads), so wider dispatch elsewhere is margin rather than dependence, and Chrome enables WebGPU for its GPU on Linux. Each row names its benchmark file in `oracles/plt/`, cache state, render resolution and percentile. Other OSes' mid machines must land within 1.5× of each row; only the reference laptop blocks beta promotion.

**Section:** PLT Performance engineering, Budgets; UIX Performance, telemetry and quality, Interaction budgets
**Problem:** The budget table mixes rows that hold, rows that hold only once their workload is defined, and rows that cannot hold on the reference laptop. All of them block beta promotion, so infeasible rows will either block every release or be waived case by case.
**Evidence:** PLT Continuous benchmarking item 4: "Any budget row exceeded on any reference machine blocks promotion of the build to beta". The titles of Chrome's "What's New in WebGPU" entries from Chrome 135 to 156 include no 64-bit atomics feature (developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/webgpu/news). UIX's own latency target is "≤ 2 frames plus display scan-out", which exceeds 33 ms at 60 Hz.

2. Define, then keep: exact rebuild 2 s on a named GP1-class benchmark of prismatic features, plus p90 ≤ 10 s on an ABC-derived 200-feature corpus; interactive simulation update 1 s for linear static elasticity up to 100,000 DOFs at p = 2, warm-started, on G1; orbit 60 fps at 5M visible triangles at 2.1 MP render resolution (R6-10).
3. Replace: coarse drag preview per R6-09; browser orbit with WebGPU 30 fps at 5M or 60 fps at 2M visible triangles; WebGL2 30 fps at 2M visible triangles and at most 1,000 distinct Parts; browser selection ≤ 33 ms (WebGPU readback resolves asynchronously) or a CPU ray cast as on G3; browser interactive simulation 2 s with WebGPU, 6 s on CPU-only sessions, remote above that; input-to-photon p99 ≤ 50 ms at 60 Hz and ≤ 33 ms at 120 Hz; native idle memory 300 MiB with the engine's GPU device created lazily (R6-16); browser idle memory measured after a heavy-worker recycle (R6-14).
4. Low-band rows stay, except the drag preview, which follows R6-09.

**Section:** UIX Direct manipulation, Coarse-first preview pipeline; KLN Scheduling and parallelism (drag lane); ANV Performance targets; PLT Budgets
**Problem:** "Coarse drag preview under 100 ms" with "dependent features updated" cannot hold for an early edit in a 200-feature part, because every downstream feature re-evaluates. Anvil's own exact targets give 50 ms to one 500-face Boolean and 100 ms to one 50-edge fillet chain; even at Preview tolerance, 150 dependents fit in 100 ms only at under 0.7 ms each.
**Evidence:** UIX: "only the edited Part's downstream features are re-evaluated", which for an early edit is nearly all of them. ANV Performance targets: "≤ 50 ms exact" and "≤ 100 ms exact" for single operations. PLT Budgets holds both "Coarse drag preview under 100 ms" and "Exact rebuild, 200-feature part, early edit under 2 s".
**Fix:** State the preview scope in UIX, KLN and ANV: within 100 ms the drag lane recomputes the dragged feature and as many dependents as Kiln's cost estimate fits in 80 ms (at least the next 10 when they are cheap). Later dependents show their previous geometry as Proxy where the change is affine on them, otherwise as Stale. After release, the 2 s exact-rebuild row applies. `uix_drag_preview_budget` runs a late-edit script and an early-edit script separately and reports how many dependents each preview covered.

**Section:** UIX Renderer, Frame budgets; UIX Transparency; PLT Budgets (orbit row)
**Problem:** The frame budget is set at 1920×1080, but the macOS mid machine (a MacBook Pro) and many Windows laptops drive panels of about 4 to 8 MP at their default scale. Resolve, edges, ambient occlusion, transparency and anti-aliasing scale with pixel count, so the 6.0 ms of pixel-proportional GPU work grows to about 17 ms on a 5.9 MP panel (2.8× the pixels), and 60 fps fails before geometry cost is counted.
**Evidence:** UIX Frame budgets at 1920×1080: resolve and edges 2.5 ms; ambient occlusion, transparency and overlays 2.5 ms; tone map, filter and composite 1.0 ms. UIX cites XeGTAO at "about 2.39 ms on an Intel i7-1195G7 integrated GPU" at 1080p. UIX switches the k-buffer to k = 2 only "above 8 megapixels".
**Fix:** Add a render-scale policy to UIX: during camera motion the 3D view renders at most 2.1 MP and upsamples, while edges, overlays and text draw at native resolution; still frames accumulate at native resolution, which D-UIX-12 already does. State every frame-budget row per render megapixel, add "60 fps at native resolution" as a high-band row, and give X-ray views their own 30 fps row (R6-27).

**Section:** UIX Renderer, GPU capability tiers; UIX Frame budgets; UIX Very large assemblies
**Problem:** G1 promises 1,000,000 Instances at 60 fps on the reference laptop with 1.0 ms for instance culling, cluster culling and the LOD cut together. Reading 1M transforms of 64 bytes moves 64 MB per frame, about half a millisecond of an integrated GPU's shared memory bandwidth before any cluster work. G2 promises 100,000 Instances in browsers that expose no 64-bit atomics, and G3 promises 10,000 Instances on WebGL2, where each distinct Part costs draw calls.
**Evidence:** UIX: "40,000 transforms of 64 bytes each"; Core Ultra 7 258V uses LPDDR5X-8533 on 2 channels (Intel ARK); the bandwidth figure is my arithmetic for a 128-bit bus. MEC sets the reference-laptop target at a "100,000-instance assembly … orbit it at 60 fps". Chrome's WebGPU entries through Chrome 156 list no 64-bit atomics.
**Fix:** Change UIX's tier table (60 fps, reference laptop, 1920×1080): G1 100,000 Instances and 5M visible triangles; G1 on the high band 1,000,000 Instances; G2 20,000 Instances and 2M visible triangles; G3 1,000 distinct Parts, or 10,000 Instances of at most 1,000 distinct Parts, and 2M visible triangles. Keep 10 million Instances as a phase 5 high-band target only. Split the 1.0 ms culling row into instance culling and cluster culling, with per-tier figures measured in phase 2.

**Section:** PLT Wasm component runtime (Status as of October 2026; Wasmtime configuration); PLT Platform notes; CONTRACT §7.4 Wasm execution
**Problem:** Every Ingot feature and Wasm component on desktop runs on Wasmtime, but Wasmtime's own tiers rate two Crucible Tier 1 targets below its Tier 1: Windows ARM64 is Tier 3 and Apple silicon macOS is Tier 2. The Tier 2 tablet targets iOS and Android are Tier 3 and Pulley is Tier 2. Tier status governs CI coverage and fuzzing, which a sandbox for third-party packages needs, and PLT's risk tables omit it.
**Evidence:** docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-tiers: `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` Tier 3 (missing "CI testing, full-time maintainer"); `aarch64-apple-darwin` Tier 2 (missing "Continuous fuzzing"); `aarch64-apple-ios` and `aarch64-linux-android` Tier 3 (missing "CI testing, full-time maintainer"); Pulley Tier 2 (missing "More time fuzzing/baking"). docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-release: security bugs reach all supported releases, while "Bug fixes are backported on a volunteer basis".
**Fix:** Add one row per affected target to PLT Platform notes. Budget one engineer from phase 0 for upstream Wasmtime work: continuous fuzzing on aarch64 macOS, CI and maintainer coverage for Windows ARM64, and iOS and Android CI, aiming for Wasmtime Tier 2 or better on both desktop ARM64 targets by the phase 1 gate. Until then, run third-party evaluation components out of process on those targets (ECO already allows this by policy) and keep Windows ARM64 in Tier 1 preview (R6-06).

**Section:** PLT Tablets and phones; PLT Open questions 1; CONTRACT §14 (No-JIT execution ruling); ECO The extension model, Running on every platform
**Problem:** The plan runs all Wasm, Ingot included, on Pulley on iPadOS and treats App Review as one open question. Pulley carries "a ~10x order-of-magnitude slowdown" and is "likely not suitable for compute-intensive tasks", and guideline 4.7 attaches obligations that no tab plans for to any software not embedded in the binary. A store-like package browser is itself unacceptable under 3.2.2(i).
**Evidence:** App Review Guidelines: 2.5.2 forbids downloading code "which introduces or changes features or functionality of the app"; 4.7 allows "HTML5 and JavaScript mini apps and mini games, streaming games, chatbots, and plug-ins" subject to 4.7.1 (privacy, filtering, reporting and blocking), 4.7.2 (no exposure of native APIs without permission), 4.7.4 ("an index of software and metadata … universal links") and 4.7.5 (age restriction); 3.2.2(i) rejects "an interface for displaying third-party apps, extensions, or plug-ins similar to the App Store"; 4.2.3(ii) requires disclosing first-launch downloads. `com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit` lists availability on macOS only (developer.apple.com). Pulley quotes from docs.wasmtime.dev/examples-pulley.
**Fix:** (1) Amend the no-JIT ruling: on iPadOS, Ingot and Wasm components run inside WebKit (a WKWebView worker, or the web build in a thin WKWebView shell), where JavaScriptCore runs WebAssembly in WebKit's own process as it does in Safari; Pulley stays the fallback. A phase 3 spike measures WKWebView memory limits, WebAssembly speed and WebGPU availability before the shell is fixed. (2) Ship std and first-party components inside the app binary. (3) Offer registry packages on iPadOS only as dependencies of an opened design, never as a browsable catalog, and meet 4.7.1, 4.7.4 and 4.7.5 (registry index with universal links, reporting, age ratings) and guideline 3.1 for paid packages. (4) Disclose first-launch downloads per 4.2.3(ii). (5) Keep remote evaluation as the path if review rejects downloaded components.

**Section:** PLT The browser target, Memory; KLN Memory management and eviction; UIX Very large assemblies (budgets) and Interaction budgets; PLT Budgets
**Problem:** WebAssembly linear memory never shrinks, so one large evaluation leaves the engine worker at its peak for the rest of the session, and the browser idle-memory row cannot hold. The tabs also disagree on the budget: PLT sets a 3 GiB residency budget, KLN a 2 GiB browser budget, and UIX adds up to 1.5 GiB of UI memory plus a 512 MiB GPU page pool, more than many tabs survive.
**Evidence:** WebAssembly memory-control overview: "WebAssembly memory can only grow and never shrink, and there are no APIs for releasing memory to the host"; the proposal "is in its early stages". PLT: "The residency manager's budget is 3 GiB on desktop browsers"; KLN: "2 GiB in browsers"; UIX: "UI memory, 1,000-part assembly ≤ 1.5 GiB host memory"; PLT Budgets browser column: "Idle memory … Under 300 MiB".
**Fix:** PLT owns one browser memory table, replacing KLN's and UIX's numbers. The engine worker keeps a fixed linear-memory cap (proposed 1.5 GiB). Evaluations whose estimated peak exceeds 512 MiB run in a disposable heavy worker with its own memory and compute workers, write results to the OPFS CAS, and terminate afterwards. Phase 0 measures the out-of-memory kill threshold of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari on 8 GB and 32 GB machines, and sets UI, engine and heavy-worker caps below it; where the sum would exceed it, heavy evaluations go remote. The browser idle-memory row is measured after a heavy-worker recycle.

**Section:** PLT The browser target (Process and thread layout; Storage); KLN Deployment, Modes (browser metadata store)
**Problem:** Neither tab says what happens when a user opens Crucible in two tabs of one origin. The browser CAS, journal and metadata store depend on OPFS synchronous access handles, which take an exclusive lock per file, and on SQLite VFSs that refuse a second instance, so the second tab fails or corrupts state.
**Evidence:** MDN `createSyncAccessHandle`: creating a handle "takes an exclusive lock on the file", and a second `readwrite` handle throws `NoModificationAllowedError`. sqlite.org persistence: the `opfs` VFS needs `SharedArrayBuffer` and "no two database handles can have the same OPFS-hosted database open at one time"; `opfs-sahpool` fails when initialized "via two tabs to the same origin". KLN: "SQLite compiled to Wasm over the Origin Private File System".
**Fix:** Specify one engine per origin. The first tab's engine worker takes a Web Lock and owns every OPFS write handle (CAS packs, journal, SQLite on `opfs-sahpool`, which also works without cross-origin isolation). Other tabs run the UI module only and reach the owner's engine through a `MessagePort` brokered by a `SharedWorker`; when the owner closes, the next tab takes the lock and replays the journal. Add a two-tab oracle: edit in both tabs, close the owner, verify that no Change is lost.

**Section:** PLT The compute runtime, GPU compute and Process model (D-PLT-12); KLN Cancellation; FLX Execution, Placement and scheduling; UIX Field visualization (per-pixel evaluation)
**Problem:** Dispatch limits disagree (PLT 100 ms, KLN 50 ms, FLX 4 ms while the camera moves), and the two larger values stall the renderer, because the engine's compute device and the UI's render device share one GPU and the OS arbitrates between the two processes. wgpu's feature list offers external memory only for Vulkan, so on DX12 and Metal, the Windows and macOS defaults, every GPU-computed Field or preview that the UI paints round-trips through host memory and is uploaded twice.
**Evidence:** PLT: "Each dispatch is sized to finish within 100 ms"; KLN: "GPU work is split into dispatches of at most 50 ms"; FLX: "solver dispatches stay under 4 ms while the camera moves, so orbit holds 60 fps". wgpu 30.0.1 lists only `VULKAN_EXTERNAL_MEMORY_WIN32`, `VULKAN_EXTERNAL_MEMORY_FD` and `VULKAN_EXTERNAL_MEMORY_DMA_BUF` for external memory (docs.rs/wgpu, Features).
**Fix:** PLT owns one rule, cited by KLN and FLX: dispatches ≤ 4 ms while any window renders interactively, ≤ 16 ms while views are idle, ≤ 100 ms only in headless processes. Display-only GPU work (per-pixel Field evaluation, implicit preview, display isosurfaces) runs on the UI process's device from coefficient buffers passed through the existing memory-mapped rings. The engine creates its GPU device lazily, so the idle-memory row excludes it, and UIX's frame budget states a copy budget (for example ≤ 5 ms per 100 MB on unified-memory laptops).

**Section:** CONTRACT §7.3 Determinism (mechanisms); PLT Numerical determinism (D-PLT-18); FLX Kernel generation (D-FLX-8), State of the art (high-order operator evaluation), Open questions 1
**Problem:** Banning FMA outside `detmath` halves peak arithmetic throughput on every x86-64-v3, x86-64-v4 and ARM64 core for kernels built from multiply-add chains (sum factorization at p ≥ 3, dense factorization, NURBS evaluation, implicit tapes), to protect the two targets that lack FMA, x86-64-v2 and wasm32. FLX nonetheless targets "at least 80% of MFEM/libCEED throughput … despite deterministic reductions and no FMA", which is infeasible for compute-bound bake-off problems, and no other tab budgets the cost.
**Evidence:** An FMA retires two flops per lane per instruction; a separate multiply and add retire the same two flops in two instructions on the same ports, so compute-bound peak halves. Core WebAssembly SIMD has no FMA; it exists only as relaxed `madd`, evaluated either "for a total of 2 roundings" or "only rounded once (if supported by hardware)", and "given the same inputs, two calls to the same instruction can return different results" (relaxed-simd Overview). FLX caps the acceptable cost at 1.3× and defers the decision to phase 0 (FLX open question 1).
**Fix:** (1) FLX replaces the target: on CPU, BP3 and BP5 at p ≥ 3 reach at least 50% of MFEM/libCEED on the reference laptop, and memory-bound cases (BP1, BP2, p ≤ 2) at least 80%. (2) Phase 0 measures the no-FMA penalty for four kernel families (sum factorization at p = 2 to 6, dense LU, NURBS evaluation, implicit tapes) and publishes it in PLT's State of the art table. (3) A family that loses more than 1.3× may ship a `CpuIsa` variant with FMA for Preview and Interactive fidelity, as D-PLT-20 and §7.3 already permit, recomputing canonically for sign-off; Kiln's cost model counts the recompute.

**Section:** CONTRACT §7.3 Determinism (mechanisms); PLT The compute runtime, SIMD (D-PLT-15); KLN Sources of nondeterminism (SIMD width row)
**Problem:** The contract and D-PLT-15 make every canonical kernel compute on 512-bit virtual vectors. On the x86-64-v2 baseline, and in browsers on x86 hosts, each virtual vector occupies four of only 16 vector registers, leaving four live vectors before spilling. Element-wise kernels gain nothing from a fixed layout, because each lane's arithmetic is independent of width; only horizontal operations need a canonical order, as KLN already states.
**Evidence:** KLN: "Element-wise kernels are width-independent by construction; reductions use a canonical order defined by data indices, not lanes (D-KLN-13)". D-PLT-15: "four 128-bit registers on NEON, SSE and SIMD128". x86-64 without AVX-512 has 16 vector registers; AArch64 has 32.
**Fix:** Replace the §7.3 phrase "fixed 512-bit virtual vectors (8 × f64, 16 × f32) mapped onto NEON, SSE, AVX2, AVX-512 and SIMD128" with "a canonical lane order for horizontal operations: every horizontal reduction, scan or cross-lane operation in `Portable` code follows the 8-lane (f64) or 16-lane (f32) tree of `det_sum`; element-wise code may use any native vector width". Rewrite D-PLT-15 and the `CanonicalSimd` trait to match: width-generic element-wise operations plus `reduce_canonical`.

**Section:** PLT Numerical determinism, The deterministic math library (D-PLT-17 and targets); PLT Phasing (phase 0 `detmath`)
**Problem:** PLT cites glibc's adoption of CORE-MATH as "a sign that its speed is acceptable in production libraries", but glibc adopted it only for seven less speed-critical binary64 functions and kept its own exp, log, sin, cos and pow. The work is also larger than phase 0 implies: about 30 functions in two precisions, each with a scalar path, an FMA-free path whose error analysis must be redone, and a batched SIMD path, while the whole determinism suite waits on them.
**Evidence:** CORE-MATH project page: "seven binary64 functions are integrated into the GNU libc up from release 2.43" (acosh, asinh, atanh, erf, erfc, lgamma, tgamma); binary32 functions from 2.42; "AMD libm (since 4.2) integrates tanhf"; the page lists crmvec, "a vector library using CORE-MATH routines", as an external project. PLT relies on "FMA-free double-double paths" for x86-64-v2 and wasm32.
**Fix:** (1) Correct the evidence sentence. (2) To unblock the determinism suite by month 3, build CORE-MATH's C sources (MIT) behind the `detmath` API with clang for every target including wasm32, with `-ffp-contract=off`; where the C code uses fused multiply-add on targets without hardware FMA, the correctly rounded C `fma` keeps the bits identical at lower speed. (3) Port to Rust one function at a time, hot functions first (exp, ln, pow, sin, cos, atan2), and evaluate batched paths against crmvec. (4) Staff two numerics specialists for 24 months (R6-03). (5) Targets per function: scalar exp and ln ≤ 1.5× and pow, sin and cos ≤ 2× glibc 2.43 on x86-64-v3; wasm32 per-call cost ≤ 3× native; batched ≥ 2× scalar on AVX2.

**Section:** PLT Wasm component runtime, The instrumentation pass (D-PLT-22); ECO The extension model, Determinism contract (determinizer step 2; overhead targets); CONTRACT §7.4
**Problem:** The determinizer inserts a NaN check after every floating-point instruction that can produce a NaN, scalar and SIMD, which is the approach Wasmtime says "adds overhead to Wasm's floating-point instructions"; in float-SIMD code it adds two or three instructions per arithmetic instruction. PLT's ≤ 10% total overhead and ECO's ≤ 15% plus ≤ 10% disagree, and neither is credible for slicers, nesting or solver components.
**Evidence:** ECO determinizer step 2: "After every floating-point instruction that can produce a NaN, insert code that replaces any NaN with the canonical quiet NaN of its type"; PLT canonicalizes "the outputs of every float SIMD operation"; Wasmtime deterministic-execution guide. PLT targets "at most 10% over uninstrumented code"; ECO targets "under 15% … and under 10% for NaN canonicalization".
**Fix:** Canonicalize only where NaN bits become observable: float stores, `reinterpret`, the sign operand of `copysign`, host-call arguments and results, and any v128 value produced by a float operation that reaches a bitwise, integer-lane, byte-shuffle, store or extract-to-integer instruction, found by a forward type-tracking pass over v128 values. Arithmetic, comparisons, `min`, `max` and float conversions never expose payload bits, so intermediate NaNs need no rewrite. PLT, which owns the determinizer under §7.4, publishes one target table that ECO cites: scalar-float components ≤ 10%, SIMD-float components ≤ 25%, fuel and stack metering ≤ 10%, measured per component class.

**Section:** PLT Numerical determinism, Third-party numerical libraries; FLX Solvers, Sparse direct solvers; FLX State of the art (sparse direct row)
**Problem:** PLT admits faer to canonical mode only in a qualified configuration such as "sequential execution with fixed block sizes", so every canonical sign-off factorization runs on one core, while FLX targets "within 2× of CHOLMOD". faer documents nothing about thread-count independence, and its parallel backend is global rayon parallelism.
**Evidence:** docs.rs faer 0.24.4: the `rayon` feature "enables global parallelism by default"; no statement on determinism or reproducibility appears. PLT: "for example sequential execution with fixed block sizes inside a deterministic combinator".
**Fix:** FLX and PLT specify a canonical parallel factorization in `flux-solve`: supernodal or multifrontal elimination with tree-level parallelism, each supernode's updates applied in a fixed child order, and dense supernode kernels with fixed blocking and canonical horizontal order, so results do not depend on thread count; offer it upstream to faer as a deterministic parallel mode. Until it exists, the CHOLMOD target applies to `CpuIsa` runs, and canonical sign-off factorization targets "within 2× of single-threaded CHOLMOD".

**Section:** CONTRACT §7.5 Shared kernel IR; FLX Kernel generation (D-FLX-9, D-FLX-10); PLT GPU compute
**Problem:** The kernel IR must serve weak forms, constitutive functions, analytic Fields, implicit tapes, constraint residuals, Network residuals and Verilog-A device models, with algorithmic differentiation and four back ends. It sits on the critical path of Flux (phase 0), Anvil's implicit lattices (phase 1) and the constraint solver, yet no tab assigns its team, a freeze date or a phase-limited construct set. One back end targets CubeCL, which is alpha software with breaking changes between minor versions.
**Evidence:** CONTRACT §7.5 lists the sources and back ends. CubeCL README: "CubeCL is currently in alpha" and "you should expect breaking changes between minor versions". wgpu `SHADER_F64` "Enables 64-bit floating point types in SPIR-V shaders" on Vulkan (docs.rs/wgpu 30.0.1).
**Fix:** (1) FLX owns a kernels team of three compiler engineers from month 0 (R6-03). (2) IR v0 freezes at month 6 with only the constructs phases 0 and 1 need: element kernels with sum factorization, pointwise constitutive functions with forward-mode derivatives, and implicit tapes; Network, constraint and Verilog-A constructs join in the phases that need them, with constraint residuals hand-written in the IR's Rust embedding meanwhile. (3) Back ends: ahead-of-time Rust and Wasm SIMD128 in phase 0; WGSL in phase 1 for interactive elasticity and implicit preview only. (4) Amend §7.5 to drop CubeCL until phase 4; server f64 GPU paths first use wgpu on Vulkan with `SHADER_F64`, and a CUDA or HIP back end is reconsidered at the phase 4 gate.

**Section:** UIX UI toolkit, Choice (D-UIX-3); UIX Open questions 1; UIX Code and visual together, The code panel; ING Tooling, Language service
**Problem:** UIX decides between its own toolkit and Masonry "at the phase 1 gate after a two-week spike", by which time the own toolkit, code editor, IME and accessibility layers will have absorbed about 20 EY. The code panel must also compete with the editors code-CAD users already work in, which is a product of its own.
**Evidence:** UIX open question 1 and D-UIX-3. Zed's editor, built on its own toolkit, reached Windows on 15 October 2025 with a dedicated Windows team (zed.dev). AccessKit's web adapter is "planned", and its adapters "don't yet support rich text or hypertext" (github.com/AccessKit/accesskit).
**Fix:** (1) Move the decision to month 3 of phase 0: a six-week bake-off builds three screens with both options (a virtualized 1,000,000-row tree, a properties panel with an IME text field, a code panel on a 50,000-line file) on Windows, macOS, Linux and Chrome, judged by `uix_a11y_tree`, `uix_ime` and the frame budgets. (2) Phase 1 toolkit scope: docked layout with collapsible panels, no detached windows, bidirectional text but no layout mirroring until phase 2, no Vim mode. (3) ING ships the language service as an LSP server over stdio in phase 1, with first-party VS Code and Zed extensions and a custom request that drives Crucible's viewport for cross-probing. The in-app code panel then covers editing, diagnostics, hover, completion and scrubbing in phase 1.

**Section:** UIX Renderer, Frame pipeline (G1 and G2), Transparency; UIX Phasing (phases 0 and 1)
**Problem:** Phases 0 and 1 build a visibility-buffer pipeline for G1 and G2, a forward pipeline for G3 and hybrid transparency, although both phase 1 golden products are single Parts. The cluster-DAG pipeline is still unfinished in its open reference implementation and belongs with the first assembly golden products.
**Evidence:** UIX Phasing: phase 0 "wgpu renderer on G1 and G3", phase 1 "browser on G2 and G3", phase 2 "Cluster DAG streaming and two-pass occlusion culling at assembly scale". Bevy's virtual geometry on wgpu: "I'm still not done working on DAG quality" and "culling is the biggest bottleneck at the moment" (jms55.github.io, 27 March 2025).
**Fix:** Phase 1 ships one forward renderer on G1, G2 and G3: per-face and per-Instance id targets for picking, model edges from `DisplayPackage`, level-0 clusters with per-Part discrete LOD, weighted blended transparency, section caps, half-resolution ambient occlusion, and Keeter-style direct implicit rendering on G1 and G2 for the GP2 lattice. The visibility buffer, DAG LOD cut, two-pass occlusion, compute rasterization and k-buffer arrive in phase 2, gated by `uix_frame_budget` on GP3 and GP4. `DisplayPackage` carries DAG pages from phase 0, so no format changes.

**Section:** ING Compilation strategy (D-ING-13; Performance targets and evidence plan); CONTRACT §14 (No-JIT execution ruling)
**Problem:** Phase 1 requires a Wasm code generator with Perceus reference counting, a state-machine transform for suspension, compiled-in fuel and bit-identical agreement with the interpreter on every target. Ingot's own budget of 200 µs per feature is within an interpreter's reach for orchestration code, so the code generator adds a second executor to the critical path with no phase 1 golden-product need.
**Evidence:** ING: "Interpreter within 15× of compiled code"; "Ingot code, excluding operations, takes at most 2% of the contract's 2 s rebuild … 200 µs per feature"; ING-O-1 compares both executors bit for bit on every target.
**Fix:** Amend the ruling: "Until the Ingot code generator ships, the reference interpreter is the only Ingot executor on every target; Pulley and browser engines run Wasm components only." ING phase 1 drops the code generator, Perceus and the state-machine transform, and adds an interpreter target (≤ 200 µs per GP1 feature body on the reference laptop, ≤ 3× that in browsers). The code generator enters phase 2 if `ingot-bench` shows Ingot above 2% of a golden-product rebuild; heavy numeric loops go to operations or `#[ingot::feature]` Rust components meanwhile.

**Section:** UIX Interfaces with other subsystems (headless snapshots); UIX Renderer, GPU capability tiers; AGT Platform notes (Determinism); AGT Oracles (O-AGT-3)
**Problem:** UIX promises `render_snapshot` "deterministic per platform class on the CPU path", and AGT requires CPU renders "byte-identical within a platform class". The CPU path is Mesa lavapipe or WARP, whose shader code is generated at run time for the host CPU, and `CpuCanonical` spans every CPU, so the promise cannot hold; macOS has no software renderer at all.
**Evidence:** Mesa llvmpipe documentation: "a software rasterizer that uses LLVM to do runtime code generation", with `LP_NATIVE_VECTOR_WIDTH` and `GALLIUM_OVERRIDE_CPU_CAPS` changing the code it emits (docs.mesa3d.org/drivers/llvmpipe.html). UIX: "Headless servers and broken drivers render through wgpu on software Vulkan (Mesa lavapipe on Linux) or WARP".
**Fix:** Declare snapshots non-canonical: they carry `PlatformClass::Unverified` plus the renderer identity, never enter cache keys or Approval digests, and are compared by ꟻLIP thresholds. Byte identity applies only on one pinned CI renderer image (a container with a pinned lavapipe build and fixed `LP_NATIVE_VECTOR_WIDTH` and `GALLIUM_OVERRIDE_CPU_CAPS`); reword O-AGT-3 accordingly. Snapshots attached to Proposals are stored once as Assets, so reviewers and approvals see the same bytes.

**Section:** UIX Renderer, Transparency (D-UIX-11)
**Problem:** The k-buffer orders layers with 32-bit atomics on depth alone, so coincident faces, common in X-ray views of assemblies where mating faces touch, tie and resolve in varying order, which shows as flicker between frames. Its memory, 41 bytes per pixel at k = 4, exceeds WebGPU's default 128 MiB storage binding on any panel above about 3.3 MP, well below the 8 MP switch to k = 2.
**Evidence:** D-UIX-11: "a two-pass k-buffer built from 32-bit atomics", "41 bytes per pixel for k = 4 (85 MB at 1920×1080)", "k = 2 above 8 megapixels on G2"; UIX Browser specifics: default `maxStorageBufferBindingSize` of 128 MiB. A 5.9 MP panel needs about 243 MB at k = 4 (my arithmetic).
**Fix:** Pack each 32-bit key as 24 bits of quantized reversed-Z depth plus an 8-bit hash of (Instance, face), and break remaining ties by `EntityId` order in the resolve pass; opaque depth stays f32. Choose k per frame from the adapter's `maxStorageBufferBindingSize` and the render resolution (R6-10), splitting bindings where the adapter allows. X-ray views get their own 30 fps row that includes the second geometry pass.

**Section:** CONTRACT §7.3 (continuous verification); PLT Build and release engineering, CI matrix; PLT The determinism suite
**Problem:** The merge queue promises, within 45 minutes per commit, builds and unit tests on every Tier 1 target, the full canonical determinism suite on every Tier 1 CPU target and in Chrome, Firefox and Safari, and golden-product checks. As the corpus grows to golden-product sign-off simulations, this needs a large farm of macOS and ARM64 machines and holds every merge behind the slowest runner; Safari cannot run headless.
**Evidence:** PLT CI matrix, merge queue row; CONTRACT §7.3: "verified continuously by a cross-platform determinism suite on every commit".
**Fix:** Amend §7.3: "The determinism suite runs on every merge on a representative set (Linux x86-64 with forced v2, v3 and v4; Linux ARM64; macOS ARM64; wasm32 in Node and headless Chrome, threaded and single-threaded) and on every other Tier 1 target and browser engine at least nightly. A nightly divergence bisects automatically, opens a severity-1 determinism incident and blocks promotion to beta, not the merge queue." Golden-product sign-off runs move to nightly. PLT adds a CI capacity line per phase (cores, macOS and ARM64 runners, GPU-lab machines) to the program plan (R6-01).

**Section:** AGT The agent API, Rate, cost and size limits; AGT Safety and security, Cost caps; AGT Oracles (O-AGT-11); KLN Kiln: incremental evaluation, Cost accounting; PLT Interfaces with other subsystems (`ResourceUsage`)
**Problem:** Admission control relies on per-operation cost models that are "linear regressions on input sizes", but adaptive solves, certified geometry with predicate escalation and Wasm components vary in cost by orders of magnitude at one input size. O-AGT-11 promises that spend never exceeds a cap by more than "one Op's metering granularity", which is unbounded when a direct factorization or a large Boolean has no safe point. GPU seconds per Op cannot be attributed on a GPU shared with the renderer.
**Evidence:** KLN Cost accounting: "Per-operation cost models are linear regressions on input sizes"; AGT: "At the cap, running Evaluations are cancelled and keep their partial results"; PLT lists `ResourceUsage` as "[field list to be agreed with AGT]" while AGT already defines `Usage`.
**Fix:** (1) Every Op whose estimate exceeds 10 core-seconds takes a deterministic work budget (fuel or iteration cap) derived from the remaining money budget, and exposes a safe point at least every 10 core-seconds; reaching the budget returns `BudgetExhausted` with the last checkpoint, which is environmental and never cached. (2) Admission reserves the work budget's priced upper bound, not the regression mean. (3) O-AGT-11's granularity becomes "one safe-point interval". (4) PLT adopts AGT's `Usage` fields; GPU seconds come from timestamp queries on compute-only submissions and are reported as unattributed when the device is shared.

**Section:** PLT Build and release engineering, Toolchain and dependencies (item 4); PLT The platform layer, Library choices; PLT The compute runtime, SIMD; FLX Build, wrap or avoid
**Problem:** Core paths depend on young or thinly maintained crates, with no risk register: CubeCL is alpha, winit 0.31 is in beta, faer and pulp come from one maintainer whose repository moved to Codeberg, AccessKit has no web adapter and no rich text, Parley, HarfRust and Taffy are pre-1.0, and wgpu changes its API every major release. `deps/approved.toml` records licence and maintainer status but no fallback.
**Evidence:** CubeCL README ("alpha"; breaking changes "between minor versions"); winit releases (0.31.0-beta.3 on 4 September, latest stable 0.30.13); faer README: "the project has migrated to codeberg" and the GitHub repository "is currently left as a mirror"; AccessKit README; Linebender: "Fearless SIMD v1.0 is here", with "3 years of security updates for v1.0" (linebender.org/blog/fearless-simd-1-0).
**Fix:** Extend `deps/approved.toml` with a risk class, an owning engineer, an upgrade cadence and a fork-or-replace plan for every core dependency, reviewed at each gate. Specific actions: fund faer's maintainer or vendor faer and pulp under a named Crucible owner; evaluate fearless_simd 1.0 against pulp for `simd` dispatch in phase 0; budget one wgpu upgrade per quarter (about three engineer-weeks, estimate); defer CubeCL (R6-22); keep AccessKit web-adapter work upstream with two engineers (R6-03).

**Section:** PLT Performance engineering, Reference hardware; PLT Build and release engineering, CI matrix (GPU lab); CONTRACT §9 Tier 1
**Problem:** Linux on ARM64 is a Tier 1 desktop target where "every golden product passes", but PLT's reference hardware for it is a Raspberry Pi 5 (CLI and viewer), a Graviton4 cloud VM and server VMs, none of which runs the desktop UI on a GPU. The GPU lab has no Linux ARM64 desktop GPU either, so desktop parity on that target is never tested.
**Evidence:** PLT Reference hardware, column "Linux ARM64 and servers"; PLT GPU lab list in the CI matrix section.
**Fix:** Add a Linux ARM64 desktop machine (a Snapdragon X laptop on a supported distribution, or an ARM64 workstation with an AMD GPU) to the mid band and the GPU lab. Otherwise amend §9 so Linux ARM64 is Tier 1 for servers and CLI and Tier 1 preview (R6-06) for the desktop UI until such a machine passes the golden products.

**Section:** ANV Performance, parallelism and determinism, Performance targets
**Problem:** Several Anvil rows are infeasible on the reference laptop as written. Certified SSI and the tolerance rule cost time that tolerant commercial kernels do not pay, yet a 500-face mixed Boolean gets 50 ms and a 50-edge fillet chain 100 ms. "Exact mesh at 50 µm chord in ≤ 10 s" for the lattice bracket implies on the order of 10⁸ triangles, which also breaks the memory row for a golden product.
**Evidence:** ANV targets table; PLT Budgets: "Memory with golden product 1 open: under 1 GiB"; MFG slices implicit lattices directly without meshing (MFG Slicing and toolpath strategies, D-MFG-11). The triangle count follows from 10⁵ TPMS cells carrying thousands of triangles each at 50 µm chord (my estimate).
**Fix:** Revise: Boolean of two 500-face mixed bodies ≤ 200 ms; 50-edge constant-radius fillet chain ≤ 500 ms; tessellation, interference and tetrahedralization rows unchanged. Replace the lattice mesh row with "direct slicing of the GP2 lattice at 50 µm without a global mesh ≤ 60 s, peak memory ≤ 2 GiB" and "mesh export at a stated triangle budget, for example 2 × 10⁷ triangles, ≤ 60 s on the high band". Add the p90 rebuild row on an ABC-derived 200-feature corpus (R6-08).

**Section:** ING Compilation strategy, Performance targets and evidence plan; FLX Kernel generation (D-FLX-9); PLT State of the art (Wasm runtime and Browser engine rows); PLT The browser target, Performance relative to native
**Problem:** Several ratio targets ignore costs the same drafts impose. Ingot is "within 1.5× of Rust natively" while generated code checks for non-finite values before every comparison and branch, checks integer overflow and counts references; Wasm components are "at most 1.3 times in Wasmtime, 2.0 times in browsers" after instrumentation; user forms are "within 2× of ahead-of-time kernels" while running 128-bit SIMD against 512-bit ahead-of-time code on AVX-512 machines; and the browser suite targets 1.6× and 2.0× native while losing wide vectors everywhere.
**Evidence:** ING The deterministic Wasm subset (NaN checks, overflow checks, fuel); D-FLX-9: "Wasm SIMD128 is narrower than AVX2 or AVX-512"; PLT State of the art targets; Jangda and colleagues measured browsers 45% to 55% slower than native on scalar SPEC code (cited by PLT).
**Fix:** Revise: Ingot numeric kernels ≤ 2.5× Rust natively and ≤ 4× in browsers (deferred with the code generator, R6-25); Wasm components ≤ 1.6× native Rust in Wasmtime and ≤ 2.5× in browsers after instrumentation; user forms ≤ 2× ahead-of-time kernels on AVX2 and ≤ 4× on AVX-512; browser suite geometric mean ≤ 2.0× single-threaded and ≤ 2.5× multi-threaded on the AVX2 reference laptop, with SIMD-heavy kernels reported separately at ≤ 3×.

**Section:** CONTRACT §13 Roadmap and golden products
**Problem:** Phases 2 to 7 have no size estimate, although they add the hardest domains: contact and shells, a full PCB toolchain, CFD and fluid-structure interaction, crash, composites, buildings, MEMS, marine and medical. Without one, the founder cannot see that the full program is a multi-thousand engineer-year undertaking, or decide which phases are core.
**Evidence:** Phase scopes in FLX, ELX, MFG, MEC and COV Phasing; R6-01's per-tab estimates as the base.
**Fix:** Add to §13.1 an order-of-magnitude plan (estimates, ±50%): phase 2, 24 months, 100 → 140 people, about 240 EY; phase 3, 30 months, 140 → 200 people, about 425 EY (ELX alone about 100 EY for capture, layout, routing, DRC, signal integrity and circuit simulation); phase 4, 30 months, 200 → 250 people, about 560 EY; phases 5 to 7, about 600 to 900 EY each. That places phase 4 near year 10 and phase 7 near years 17 to 19, about 3,500 to 4,000 EY in total. Treat golden products 7 to 16 as separately funded programs, each started only with a physical test partner and an approved plan, as §13 already requires for their gates.

**Section:** FLX Solvers, Determinism (item 4); FLX State of the art (reproducible reductions row); PLT Deterministic parallel combinators; KLN Determinism policy (D-KLN-13)
**Problem:** FLX uses binned accumulation for every CPU dot product and norm, while PLT and KLN reserve binned `exact_sum` for reductions whose partitioning varies and use fixed trees elsewhere. Flux already fixes virtual partitions by problem size, so binned sums buy nothing on one node and cost about 4× per reduction.
**Evidence:** FLX: "On CPUs, dot products and norms use binned accumulation as in ReproBLAS … a dot product about 4× slower than an optimized one on one core"; PLT: "`exact_sum` is reserved for global reductions in distributed solvers"; KLN D-KLN-13 rejects "always using binned summation".
**Fix:** FLX uses `det_sum` and `det_reduce` for node-local reductions and `exact_sum` only across ranks; the CG overhead target becomes ≤ 1.05× per iteration on one node.

**Section:** KLN Kiln: incremental evaluation, Cancellation; KLN Determinism policy (NaN payloads row; hardware-specific SIMD row; Requirements on the Platform tab, item 6)
**Problem:** KLN still specifies Wasmtime epoch interruption for cancellation, Cranelift NaN canonicalization, `relaxed_simd_deterministic` and a browser "loader that inserts NaN canonicalization and fuel counting". This contradicts the contract's single determinizer and its ban on epochs, and leaves two mechanisms for one job.
**Evidence:** KLN: "Wasm components are interrupted by Wasmtime epoch interruption"; item 6: "Wasmtime configured with NaN canonicalization, deterministic relaxed SIMD, fuel for limits and epochs for cancellation". CONTRACT §7.4: "Fuel, never wall-clock time, bounds work; epoch interruption is never used". PLT Wasmtime configuration: `epoch_interruption` false, `wasm_relaxed_simd` false.
**Fix:** Replace in KLN: cancellation is checked at the determinizer's fuel checkpoints; NaN canonicalization and relaxed-SIMD rejection come from the determinizer on every engine (§7.4); delete the Wasmtime settings and the browser loader from item 6 and from the two rows.

**Section:** PLT Wasm component runtime, In the browser
**Problem:** PLT transpiles each component inside the engine worker with jco, while the contract says browsers run registry-built bundles and ECO rejects client-side transpiling. In-browser transpiling also adds a JavaScript toolchain to the browser payload and a second source of browser bundles to verify.
**Evidence:** PLT: "The engine worker transpiles each instrumented Wasm component once with jco's transpiler, run inside the engine worker"; CONTRACT §7.4: "browsers run registry-built bundles in their own engines"; ECO D-ECO-10 rejects "transpiling in the client".
**Fix:** PLT: browsers load registry-built bundles; components built locally and not yet published get their browser bundle from the desktop toolchain or the team server; remove jco from the browser engine.

**Section:** PLT Performance engineering, Budgets (cold start and installed size rows); UIX Platforms and devices, Browser specifics
**Problem:** The two tabs set different browser startup and payload targets for the same measurement.
**Evidence:** PLT: "under 2.5 s with warm HTTP cache; under 8 s on a first visit over 100 Mbit/s" and "Engine download under 25 MiB compressed per build"; UIX: "interactive in 3 s on a warm HTTP cache and 6 s cold on a 50 Mbit/s link, with a Wasm payload under 20 MB compressed".
**Fix:** PLT owns one row: warm start ≤ 2.5 s; first visit ≤ 8 s at 50 Mbit/s; initial Wasm (UI module plus engine) ≤ 25 MiB brotli-compressed, with translators, CAM, electronics and physics packages loaded on demand. UIX points to it.

**Section:** PLT The platform layer, Library choices (D-PLT-4)
**Problem:** D-PLT-4 pins a 0.31 beta in phase 0 and moves to the stable release "once published", but 0.31 has been in beta since November with breaking changes in each beta and no announced date.
**Evidence:** winit releases: 0.31.0-beta.1 and beta.2 on 16 November, beta.3 on 4 September (many public enums made `#[non_exhaustive]`, a macOS window attribute removed); latest stable 0.30.13 on 2 March.
**Fix:** Pin a specific 0.31 beta commit on a Crucible-maintained patch branch with a named owner, budget half an engineer for upstream pen, IME and drag-out work, re-pin at each beta, and record the dependency in the register of R6-30.

**Section:** PLT Packaging, distribution and updates (macOS entitlement paragraph)
**Problem:** PLT says the JIT entitlement "is exercised only when a Wasm component is installed or upgraded", but mapping precompiled code as executable at every load also needs the hardened-runtime exception, and Ingot modules compiled per edit, once the code generator exists, use it continuously.
**Evidence:** Apple: the entitlement governs whether "the app may create writable and executable memory using the MAP_JIT flag", and "The Hardened Runtime disallows this by default" (developer.apple.com, `com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit`).
**Fix:** State that the entitlement is in use whenever Wasmtime loads or compiles code, and base the macOS security review on dynamic code being present in every session.

**Section:** PLT Tablets and phones (Wasm components row); ECO The extension model, Running on every platform (Android row)
**Problem:** Both tabs mark Google Play's policy on downloaded code as unverified. The policy permits code that runs in a virtual machine or interpreter with indirect API access, so Wasmtime on Android is allowed as long as components get no direct Android API access; separately, Wasmtime rates `aarch64-linux-android` Tier 3.
**Evidence:** Google Play Device and Network Abuse policy: "an app may not download executable code (such as dex, JAR, .so files) from a source other than Google Play. This restriction does not apply to code that runs in a virtual machine or an interpreter where either provides indirect access to Android APIs"; docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-tiers.
**Fix:** Replace the [unverified] marks with this citation and its condition (no world imports Android APIs directly), and add Android to the upstream Wasmtime item of R6-12.

**Section:** UIX Renderer, Display of Implicit, SubD and Mesh Bodies; ANV Performance, parallelism and determinism, GPU use
**Problem:** UIX compiles each Anvil implicit expression to WGSL for direct rendering, so every edit of a lattice parameter creates a new pipeline whose shader compile lands inside the drag. Anvil already specifies a GPU tape interpreter with interval pruning that takes new tapes as data.
**Evidence:** UIX: "Direct implicit rendering compiles the Anvil expression to WGSL"; ANV GPU use table: "Implicit tape interpreter with interval pruning".
**Fix:** UIX renders implicits with Anvil's WGSL tape interpreter during edits, and compiles a specialized shader only for still views of an unchanged expression.

**Section:** UIX UI toolkit, Text (D-UIX-4)
**Problem:** Grayscale antialiasing of unhinted 11 and 12 px text on 100%-scaled 1080p Windows and Linux displays looks soft beside native applications, and D-UIX-4 says nothing about hinting.
**Evidence:** UIX Typography sets tree rows and controls at 12 px and captions at 11 px; Skrifa's `outline` module covers "Loading, scaling and hinting of glyph outlines" (docs.rs skrifa 0.48.0).
**Fix:** Add to D-UIX-4: glyphs are hinted with Skrifa's hinter at UI scale below 1.5 on every platform, using the same code so layout and bitmaps stay identical across OSes, and unhinted above; the snapshot oracles run at both scales.

**Section:** KLN The CAS, Hashing (D-KLN-14); PLT The browser target, Storage
**Problem:** SHA-256 compiled to wasm32 has no SHA instructions, so browser hashing runs several times slower than native, and the 1 GiB in 150 ms target has no browser counterpart. Browsers offer native SHA-256 in workers.
**Evidence:** MDN `SubtleCrypto.digest`: "available in Web Workers", supports SHA-256, "returns a Promise", and "does not support streaming input".
**Fix:** The browser CAS hashes each chunk (≤ 1 MiB, already independent under D-KLN-15) with `crypto.subtle.digest` from the engine worker and combines chunk digests through `Index` nodes; state a browser target (for example 1 GiB in ≤ 1 s with 8 workers), and keep the Wasm SHA-256 for small synchronous objects.

**Section:** PLT The browser target, Cross-origin isolation
**Problem:** The isolated application must send `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin`, which severs references to cross-origin popups, so popup-based OIDC or SAML sign-in and payment flows break; the section does not say how sign-in works.
**Evidence:** MDN COOP: with `same-origin`, cross-origin documents open in a new browsing context group, and "any references between the new document and its opener are severed"; `same-origin-allow-popups` exists for "a cross-origin service for OAuth or payments".
**Fix:** Specify redirect-based sign-in for the isolated application pages, or a separate non-isolated sign-in page that hands a token to the application by same-origin redirect, and add a sign-in test with the reference identity providers to the browser-isolation oracle.

**Section:** UIX Renderer, Frame pipeline (G1 and G2), G2 paragraph
**Problem:** G2 draws visible clusters with one non-indexed `drawIndirect` that runs 384 vertex invocations per 128-triangle cluster and pads with degenerate triangles. Vertex work is therefore three invocations per triangle with no post-transform reuse, on the tier that has no compute rasterization to fall back on.
**Evidence:** UIX: "A vertex shader pulls cluster vertices from storage buffers and emits degenerate triangles past a cluster's triangle count."
**Fix:** The cluster-culling pass writes the surviving clusters' triangle indices into one compacted index buffer, drawn with a single `drawIndexedIndirect`, so shared vertices are reused and no degenerate triangles are issued; keep the per-cluster method as the fallback when the compacted buffer would exceed the binding limit.

**Section:** PLT The compute runtime, GPU compute; PLT Numerical determinism, Sources of divergence; PLT Tablets and phones
**Problem:** Several PLT [unverified] marks can now be closed, and leaving them open hides settled facts from implementers.
**Evidence:** The WGSL Candidate Recommendation Draft (w3.org/TR/WGSL, versioned 21 September 2026) contains section 15.7.5 "Reassociation and Fusion"; `com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit` lists availability on macOS only, and App Review guideline 2.5.2 forbids downloaded code that changes functionality; Google Play's virtual-machine exception (R6-41); Document-Isolation-Policy "is shipping in Chrome 137 for desktop only" (developer.chrome.com/blog/document-isolation-policy).
**Fix:** Replace those marks with these citations; keep [unverified] only on per-browser `Atomics.waitAsync` support, Windows Error Reporting local dumps and the MSIX-in-MSI mechanism.

**Section:** Contract 5 (`ErrorBound`, `ErrorBudget`), 7.1 Flux; FLX "Calibrated estimates" (D-FLX-24); COV "Error budgets and model form" (D-COV-17); MEC "Design checks" (D-MEC-30)
**Problem:** Every phase 1 `SignOff` stress and buckling check passes on a calibrated `Estimated` bound, and that bound carries only a marginal 99% guarantee over FLX's corpus. This is the failure mode R1-04 found for surrogates, and the contract fixed it only for surrogates: topology optimization and agents that minimize mass subject to a passing check select exactly the designs where the estimator undershoots, so coverage on optimized designs falls below the corpus rate. The calibration miss rate also never enters the budget's confidence: contract 5 union-bounds only "statistical, conformal, input distributions", so a `Pass` on an η99 bound reports no confidence at all. Finally, a class is a label the model author assigns (D-COV-17), with no computable test that a given result belongs to the population the 300 samples came from.
**Evidence:** FLX D-FLX-24: η99 is "the 99th-percentile underestimate of that estimator on its problem class". FLX-O-ERR-3: "Bound at least the true error in at least 99% of held-out cases per class". MEC D-MEC-30: "physics checks accept, at `SignOff`, calibrated `Estimated` bounds". Contract 7.1 applies the selection argument only to surrogates: "inside optimization loops calibration uses weighted conformal prediction". MEC's class for GP1 and GP2, "Linear elasticity, regularized peak, immersed octree", spans every geometry, cut fraction, Poisson's ratio and distance to a singular set.
**Fix:** (1) Contract 5: `Estimated { calibration }` carries its exceedance level α (0.01 for η99) and joins the union bound with the other confidence-carrying parts, so every `CheckOutcome` reports its total confidence. (2) Each calibration class in `std::sim::calibration` carries an applicability envelope over computable estimator features: degree p, minimum cut-cell volume fraction, cells per smoothing radius (ρ/h), distance to the nearest flagged singular set in units of ρ, Poisson's ratio and material contrast. A result outside its class envelope reports `Indicator`. (3) A `SignOff` `Pass` resting on an `Estimated` discretization part needs a refinement-consistency confirmation: one further level (h/2 or p + 1) whose value lies inside the first bound and whose own bound is smaller. Kiln's cost model counts the extra solve. (4) Every class corpus includes at least 20% adversarial samples, produced by `std::opt` runs that minimize the check margin inside the class envelope, and FLX-O-ERR-3 adds an adversarial search for undershoots, as FLX-O-ROM-2 does for surrogates. (5) Contract 7.1's sentence "Interactive bounds are reported already multiplied by their calibrated factor" becomes "every `Estimated` bound", matching D-FLX-24.

**Section:** Contract 6 canonical example and 7.1 singular points; FLX "Regularized goals and singular points"; ING "Checks" outcome table
**Problem:** Three different singular-point rules exist, and under two of them the canonical check can never pass. The contract makes a point quantity `Undecided` "unless the check names a region excluding a stated distance from" every flagged set. ING makes it `Undecided` when "the region comes within the exclusion distance". FLX makes it `Undecided` when the quantity is within the exclusion distance. FLX's detector flags "edges of fixed or loaded patches", and the canonical check's region `p.away_from(clamp, 2 * thickness)` excludes the clamp but not the loaded `web.face(role: end_cap)`, so under the contract and ING the canonical example is always `Undecided { SingularPoint }`. ING's own `bracket_check` (`b.away_from(clamp, 8mm)` with a loaded `pad`) fails the same way. The detector is also blind to traction compatibility: a uniform normal traction over a whole face bounded by convex 90° edges is compatible at the corner and not singular, while a shear traction meeting a free face is.
**Evidence:** Contract 7.1: "edges of fixed or loaded patches) make point quantities `Undecided { SingularPoint }` unless the check names a region excluding a stated distance from them." Contract 6: `static_stress(p, fixed: clamp, force: load, on: web.face(role: end_cap))` and `max(over: p.away_from(clamp, 2 * thickness))`. ING table: "The region comes within the exclusion distance of a flagged singular edge | `Undecided { SingularPoint }`". At a 90° corner with traction t on face x and a free face y, equilibrium needs σ_xy = t_y on one face and σ_xy = 0 on the other, so only a shear component is incompatible.
**Fix:** State one rule in contract 7.1 and point to it from FLX and ING: (1) The detector flags a load or support patch boundary only where the prescribed condition is incompatible there: a patch boundary inside a smooth face, a corner where a shear traction meets a free face, or a clamped face meeting a free face. Re-entrant edges and material junctions stay flagged. (2) Every flagged set carries a default exclusion distance, max(2ρ, local wall thickness), which a check may override. (3) A regularized maximum is `Undecided { SingularPoint }` only when its near-maximal set (locations whose regularized value lies within the bound of the maximum) meets the exclusion zone of a flagged set; a region that merely contains a flagged set is not `Undecided`. (4) Rewrite ING's row accordingly. (5) Make the canonical example explicit about both ends: `max(over: p.away_from([clamp, web.face(role: end_cap)], 2 * thickness))`, and add an oracle that the canonical bracket decides at `SignOff`.

**Section:** Contract 7.1 Flux (local slenderness criterion); FLX "Per-region models" (`flux::mark_reduction`)
**Problem:** The R1-02 fix does not hold for its main use. L_local includes "the distance to the nearest load", so any wall carrying a distributed load has L_local = 0 and t/L_local ≤ 0.2 never holds. Pressure on enclosures, tanks, hulls and wing skins is distributed, and so are gravity and inertia. Read literally, modal analysis (a shared phase 1 capability), GP5's drop test and every pressure load mark all thin walls `Solid`. That returns them to the volumetric octree that R1-02 showed needs 10⁶ to 10⁸ DOFs.
**Evidence:** Contract 7.1: "L_local is the smallest of the span between supports, the radius of curvature and the distance to the nearest load or feature". FLX repeats it: "computed from the study's conditions and Anvil's thickness, curvature and distance queries". FLX D-FLX-12 justifies reduction by golden products 2, 4, 5 and 8, all of which carry distributed or inertial loads.
**Fix:** Replace the definition in contract 7.1 and FLX with: "L_local is the smallest of the span between supports, the radius of curvature, the distance to the nearest concentrated condition (a point or line load, the edge of a load or support patch lying inside the wall, an opening or a feature), and, for distributed loads, the length |q|/|∇q| over which the load varies. Distributed loads, body forces and inertia that cover the wall do not shorten L_local." Add plates under uniform pressure, cylinders under internal pressure and a free plate in modal analysis to FLX-O-PLAN-2 as cases that must mark `Shell`.

**Section:** Contract 13.1 phase 1 gate; COV "Evidence levels" (D-COV-3) and Open questions 3; COV Phasing phase 1
**Problem:** Phase 1 validates no physics model, so every phase 1 `SignOff` check is a conditional `Pass` whose release depends on a citable allowance catalogue that COV open question 3 leaves undecided. GP1 and GP2 measure geometry only, so no model reaches E3 under D-COV-3. All phase 1 physics stays E2 with model form `NotQuantified`, and contract 5 then needs a policy allowance "with a citation" for every check. GP2's gate also names no process, alloy or predicted quantity. The 13.4 rows that cite GP2 (strut buckling, inherent strain) therefore have no measured comparison that needs them.
**Evidence:** Contract 13.1: GP2 is "optimized and verified in Crucible; printed from Crucible's 3MF with the printer vendor's slicer; measured externally". COV phase 1: "E2 checks passing on cited allowances". COV open question 3: "Which design-code clauses state that their factors cover model uncertainty, per model class?" MFG's example build is `shop::pbf_ti64_400`, and MFG-O-AM-8 expects a "metal PBF build of GP2", but the contract never says so.
**Fix:** (1) Contract 13.1: GP1 and GP2 each add a proof-load test on three replicates, with strain gauges in each checked region and a load–displacement record, validated under V&V 10 with the V&V 20 metric. This raises immersed linear elasticity (GP1) and the beam-lattice model with localized strut stresses (GP2) to E3 in their Calibrated zones, so phase 1 releases need no allowance for those quantities. (2) Name GP2's process and alloy in 13.1, for example laser powder bed fusion of Ti-6Al-4V as MFG's example uses. (3) Answer COV open question 3: each std catalogue entry records code, edition, clause, factor, scope and whether the factor covers action-effect model uncertainty or resistance model uncertainty. Only action-effect entries cover the model form of a finite-element stress analysis. Each entry is confirmed by two non-author domain reviewers, as D-COV std review already requires. Until an entry is verified it cannot be cited.

**Section:** FLX "Budgets and guarantees", "Eigenvalue problems"; MEC D-MEC-30; contract 13.4 row 1
**Problem:** Flux defines no error budget for eigenvalues, yet the first 13.4 row and MEC's buckling checks rest on them. The budget table covers energy bounds, linear goals and regularized peaks only, so a buckling load factor or a natural frequency has no estimator and can only be `Indicator`, which never decides `SignOff`. MEC names the class "Linear buckling, Lanczos or LOBPCG", which is a solver, not an estimator. Conforming Rayleigh–Ritz approximations of the lowest eigenvalue are upper bounds for the exact pre-stress, so the discretization error lies on the unsafe side of "load factor ≥ 2" and "first frequency above the excitation band". LOBPCG also needs a positive definite B matrix, which the geometric stiffness K_G is not.
**Evidence:** FLX budget table has no eigenvalue row; the only eigen error statement is "degenerate eigenspaces are reported as subspaces with Kato–Temple bounds", an algebraic statement. MEC D-MEC-30: "Buckling load factors | Calibrated `Estimated` | Linear buckling, Lanczos or LOBPCG". Goal-oriented eigenvalue estimation exists (Heuveline and Rannacher, Adv. Comput. Math. 15, 2001, https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Heuveline+Rannacher+posteriori+error+control+eigenvalue+problems&rows=3), and so do guaranteed lower bounds for Laplace-type operators (Carstensen and Gedicke, Math. Comp. 83, 2014, https://api.crossref.org/works?query.bibliographic=Guaranteed+lower+bounds+for+eigenvalues+Carstensen+Gedicke&rows=2).
**Fix:** Add an eigenvalue row to FLX's budget table. The discretization part is the DWR eigenvalue estimate, `Estimated { calibration }` in its own class and applied on the unsafe side. `Guaranteed` lower bounds apply only where a method proves them, such as Crouzeix–Raviart-type bounds for scalar diffusion on fitted simplices, never elasticity on cut cells. The algebraic part comes from Kato–Temple or Lehmann bounds, with the gap taken from the next computed Ritz value. Buckling solves K_G φ = μ K φ with K as the positive definite B matrix and λ = 1/μ_max. MEC renames the class "linear buckling factor, eigenvalue DWR, beam lattice" (and the octree variant), and FLX-O-SOLVE-6 adds an effectivity criterion on NAFEMS free vibration and Euler columns.

**Section:** COV "Dynamics and stability" (Buckling) and "Regime variables" (Imperfection sensitivity); COV "Solid mechanics" (feature ≥ 10 grains); MFG "Slicing, lattices, process simulation and DfAM" (as-built struts)
**Problem:** GP2's strut-buckling check uses linear elastic eigen-buckling, which overestimates the capacity of typical printed lattice struts. They are stocky enough to buckle inelastically, and their as-built waviness and diameter scatter reduce capacity further. COV's envelope refuses eigen-buckling only for shells flagged imperfection-sensitive, so struts pass unchecked. Flux has no operation that computes the Koiter coefficient the regime variable needs. The as-built strut diameters MFG calibrates arrive in phase 2, after GP2. COV's default "feature ≥ 10 grains" also puts many printed struts in the Extrapolated zone, and no strut-scale Material exists to fix that.
**Evidence:** The Johnson transition slenderness is π√(2E/σ_y). With typical Ti-6Al-4V values (E ≈ 110 GPa, σ_y ≈ 900 MPa, unverified handbook figures) it is about 49. A 0.6 mm strut 3 mm long has L/r = 3/0.15 = 20, well inside the inelastic range, where Euler's load exceeds the Johnson load. COV buckling envelope: "Eigen-buckling `Refuse` at `SignOff` on shells flagged imperfection-sensitive". MFG: "as-printed strut diameters calibrated per process", phase 2. FLX defines no Koiter computation.
**Fix:** (1) COV's linear eigen-buckling envelope adds the regime variable σ_cr,Euler / σ_proportional per member: Calibrated below 0.5, `Refuse` above 1. Escalation goes to the Johnson or tangent-modulus L0 rung for struts, or to nonlinear analysis with plasticity in phase 2. (2) It adds an imperfection regime variable for struts, the waviness amplitude over the radius of gyration from MFG's as-built calibration, `Flag` above a declared value with a Perry–Robertson-type reduction as the L0 alternative. (3) MFG's as-built strut calibration for metal PBF moves to phase 1 and enters 13.4, since GP2 needs it. (4) COV ships strut-scale Materials calibrated on as-built strut specimens, whose coverage includes strut diameter, so printed lattices are not Extrapolated by the grain default. (5) FLX adds `flux::koiter_coefficient` in phase 2 with nonlinear shells. In phase 1 the shell classifier is moot because shells start in phase 2.

**Section:** Contract 13.4 row "Additive distortion by inherent strain"; FLX "Coupling" (element activation); MFG "Additive processes and build preparation", "Slicing, lattices, process simulation and DfAM"
**Problem:** Phase 1 predicts GP2's distortion with no supports, no baseplate removal and no stress relief, so the prediction cannot match what is printed and measured. Metal PBF supports are an MFG phase 2 capability. In phase 1 the vendor's slicer generates supports Crucible never sees, and the as-built shape the gate measures follows baseplate cutting, support removal and usually stress-relief heat treatment, none of which Flux models. GP2's gate compares no distortion prediction anyway (R7-04), so the 13.4 rule ("the first gate that needs it") does not put inherent strain in phase 1.
**Evidence:** MFG: "Supports | … block, line, cone and lattice supports (metal PBF) | … | MFG-O-AM-4 | 2". D-MFG-25: "In phase 1 … Crucible hands builds to the user's slicer". FLX: "Element activation switches cells on by a layer or time Field: per layer group for additive inherent strain (phase 1)". MFG-O-AM-8: "metal PBF build of GP2 within 0.1 mm in phase 2".
**Fix:** Move "Additive distortion by inherent strain" in 13.4 to phase 2, beside metal PBF supports and compensation, and update FLX, COV and MFG phasing. Specify the analysis as a declared sequence: layer-group activation of part plus supports (supports as a homogenized lattice material with calibrated stiffness), baseplate cut, support removal and optional stress relief (inherent strain scaled by a calibrated relaxation factor). Each step's data comes from MFG's coupons, for example cantilever coupons cut from the plate. If phase 1 keeps the row, the bureau's support geometry must be imported as an Asset into the build model; otherwise phase 1 states that distortion is not predicted.

**Section:** Contract 13.4 rule and rows
**Problem:** The shared phase table phases each capability by the gate that names it, but not by what it depends on. Several prerequisites therefore land after the capabilities that need them: metal PBF supports (MFG 2) after inherent strain (1); as-built strut calibration (MFG 2) after GP2's strut checks (1); `anvil::boundary_layer` (ANV 4) after the phase 3 laminar conjugate heat transfer and 3D mould fill that FLX's own plan sends to fitted boundary layers; an eigenvalue estimator (none) under row 1; and a Koiter-coefficient computation (none) under COV's buckling envelope. The SPMe row omits FLX, although SPMe needs FLX's phase 4 parameter-domain spaces.
**Evidence:** ANV: "`anvil::boundary_layer` | … | ANV-O-BL-1 | 4". FLX plan defaults: "Contact, sliding interfaces, boundary layers; voxel data | Fitted meshes; finite cell". FLX: "Parameter-domain spaces | … | FLX-O-FORM-5 | 4" and "parameter-domain forms for SPMe cells" (phase 4), while 13.4's SPMe row lists "Also phased in: COV".
**Fix:** Add to the 13.4 rule: "A capability that a row or a gate depends on takes a phase no later than its dependent; each row names its prerequisites in a column 'Needs'." Then apply it: supports and inherent strain both in phase 2 (R7-07); as-built strut calibration in phase 1 (R7-06); laminar conjugate heat transfer and mould fill state an octree wall-resolution rule instead of fitted layers (R7-09); eigenvalue DWR in phase 1 under row 1 (R7-05); a Koiter computation in phase 2 under COV's nonlinear buckling; FLX added to the SPMe row's "Also phased in".

**Section:** FLX "Solve plans and per-region discretization" (plan defaults), "Coupling" (conjugate heat transfer); MFG "Molds and injection molding" (D-MFG-15)
**Problem:** Phase 3 runs laminar conjugate heat transfer and 3D fill, pack and cool on the immersed octree, yet neither states how finely the wall-normal layers must be resolved, and FLX's plan default sends boundary layers to fitted meshes that Anvil delivers only in phase 4. The octree's only resolution rule, four cells across a section, comes from elasticity. It does not resolve a natural-convection thermal boundary layer or the frozen skin and gapwise shear profile that govern fill pressure, pack and warpage. GP5's measured warpage and hottest-part targets therefore have no defined resolution, and no estimator or GCI requirement says when the octree solution is converged.
**Evidence:** FLX: "Conjugate heat transfer | Partitioned with Robin conditions, or monolithic on a shared octree | 3 (laminar, natural convection), 4 (turbulent)". D-MFG-15: "a level-set fill front on the immersed octree for the Stokes-regime melt". ELX phase 3 evidence: "hottest part within ±5 K of measurement (targets)".
**Fix:** Amend FLX's plan default to "turbulent boundary layers needing y⁺ resolution: fitted layers from phase 4; laminar thermal layers and frozen layers: octree wall refinement". Add plan rules: at least five cells at p = 2 across δ_T = H·Ra_H^(−1/4) on heated walls, and at least eight cells across the cavity half-thickness for 3D fill and pack. Name both as regime variables in COV's convection and moulding envelopes, with under-resolution making the zone Extrapolated. Require solution verification (D-FLX-34) or an estimator for the fill-pressure and warpage goals at `SignOff`. MFG states GP5's expected 3D cell count as a target.

**Section:** Contract 5 `ErrorBudget` composition and 13.1 validation metric; COV "Error budgets and model form" (D-COV-20)
**Problem:** Validation measures model-form error on particular system response quantities, but COV applies the result to every check the model serves, and the contract gives no rule for that transfer. Strain at three gauges or a tip deflection does not bound the model error of a regularized peak stress elsewhere. Under contract 5 the bounds sit in different norms (`Goal` of the validated quantity versus `Goal` of the checked functional), so a strict reading makes every E3 total `NotQuantified`, and a loose reading transfers the bound silently. V&V 20 also needs u_num as a standard uncertainty, while Flux reports bounds (`Guaranteed`, or `Estimated` at 99%), and no tab says how to convert one into the other.
**Evidence:** COV: "E3 or E4, Calibrated | `Estimated`: |E| + k·u_val at the nearest validation points". Contract 5: "bounds in different norms never combine (the total is `NotQuantified`)". Contract 13.1: "u_val = √(u_num² + u_input² + u_D²)".
**Fix:** Add to contract 5: "A model-form bound from validation applies to a check functional J only when the validation plan lists J's response-quantity class (quantity, location type and regime) among its validated classes; otherwise the model-form part is `NotQuantified { reason: UnvalidatedQuantity }`." Then (1) COV's `ValidityEnvelope.evidence` records the validated response-quantity classes; (2) D-COV-20 states the conversion u_num = B/√3 for a `Guaranteed` bound B (uniform) and u_num = B/z_{1−α/2} for an `Estimated` bound at level α; (3) contract 13.1 requires each physical gate's validation plan to place sensors on the checked quantities (R7-04).

**Section:** FLX D-FLX-26; COV "Error budgets and model form"; contract 5 `ErrorSource`
**Problem:** Two producers fill one budget slot. `ErrorBudget.parts` is a map with one entry per `ErrorSource`, but D-FLX-26 files the shell and beam reduction error under "model form" while COV fills the same key from validation or `NotQuantified { NoValidationData }`. Which one wins decides whether every thin-wall check is a conditional `Pass`, and no rule says. The contract already has a `reduction or surrogate` source, which fits a reduction from 3D to a shell or beam. D-FLX-26 also leaves the 3D patch size unstated, though the patch must extend past the boundary layers that shell theory gets wrong.
**Evidence:** Contract 5: "`parts: map ErrorSource → Component<Q>`" and its source list includes both "model form" and "reduction or surrogate". D-FLX-26: "Dimensional-reduction error is a model-form part". COV: "E2, any zone | `NotQuantified { reason: NoValidationData }`".
**Fix:** D-FLX-26 reports the dimensional-reduction estimate under `reduction or surrogate`, and COV's model-form part keeps its meaning for the 3D constitutive and physics model. Specify the patch: it extends max(3t, 2√(R·t)) beyond the goal region (R the local radius of curvature), and the estimate is `Estimated { calibration }` in its own class, which FLX-O-PLAN-4 calibrates.

**Section:** PLT D-PLT-35; FLX "Verification, validity and agreement" (FLX-O-ERR-10)
**Problem:** The R1-12 fix does not hold: requiring |q_A − q_B| ≤ E_A + E_B lets a class drift by the whole discretization error before anyone notices. Plans are hardware-independent, so when both classes solve the same discretization the discretization error is common to both and cancels in q_A − q_B. Only the algebraic, floating-point and step-control parts differ by class, and they are orders of magnitude smaller. A GPU pipeline that is wrong by 3% still "agrees" when the discretization part is 4%. The same rule fires false severity-1 incidents: with `Estimated` parts at 99%, about 2% of correct comparisons exceed the ratio 1, and a nightly corpus of thousands of quantities produces dozens of false incidents.
**Evidence:** D-PLT-35: "E is q's `ErrorBudget` total in q's norm plus an absolute floor"; "a ratio above 1 also fails the owning tab's effectivity oracle". FLX: "Plans depend only on their inputs, never on hardware". Contract 7.3: "A nightly divergence … opens a severity-1 determinism incident".
**Fix:** Rewrite D-PLT-35: when both classes ran the same resolved `SolvePlan` and the same adaptive marks, the tolerance is the sum of each class's algebraic, floating-point and temporal-control parts plus the absolute floor. Full budgets apply only when marks differ, and diverging marks are reported as their own finding.
