**Section:** Contract 5 `Labels`, 7.1 `repo`, 7.6 "Context labels and write-down", 7.8; AGT "Labels and injection defence"; KLN "Labels and export control", "Encryption at rest", "Live documents"
**Problem:** Contract 5 puts `integrity` inside one product lattice whose join is "the union of each set", and 7.6 fails every write "to a destination with a lower label" unless two people, one an export officer, sign a declassification. Integrity flags therefore count as "higher": a `data_untrusted` context editing its own branch of a clean repository is a write-down, which contradicts AGT's Rule-of-Two table ("Edit own branch: Yes"). Conversely `propose.endorse_text` lowers a span's integrity with one human, while KLN says "Lowering a label needs a declassification record signed by two people, one an export officer". The same lattice keys encryption domains and live-replication units, so every combination of integrity flags becomes its own domain and its own Loro document, and the read rule ("a principal may read a value only if it satisfies every element") has no meaning for integrity.
**Evidence:** Contract 5: "The join takes the maximum level and the union of each set. A principal may read a value only if it satisfies every element." Contract 7.6: "A write to a destination with a lower label fails with `label.write_down` unless a declassification record signed by two people, one of them an export officer, names it." AGT "Taint and the Rule of Two" allows `data_untrusted` and `instruction_tainted` contexts to edit their own branch. Contract 7.8: "Encryption domains are keyed by tenant and canonical label set"; 7.1: "blocks labelled above a document's label live in a separate document". No tab separates integrity from these comparisons (grep of AGT and KLN for "confidentiality" finds nothing).
**Fix:** Amend contract 5: `Labels` has two parts. The confidentiality part `C = { level, controls, scopes, licences }` is a lattice with join, read rule, clearance and write-down. The integrity part `I = { instruction_tainted, data_untrusted }` joins through derivations but never blocks a read or a write; it is lowered only by endorsement (text spans, and Assets per R11-13), never by declassification. Amend 7.6: write-down compares `C` only; integrity sets risk classes and taint as AGT specifies. Amend 7.1 and 7.8: live-replication units and encryption domains key on the canonical `C` only; integrity travels as span provenance and as a per-object field. Endpoint, client and recipient clearances bound `C` only. Add to AGT-O-17: a tainted context's edit to a clean branch succeeds at R3, and an `endorse_text` changes integrity without a declassification record.

**Section:** ING free-text spans (D-ING-24) and `String`; AGT "Structured scene graph", "Sections and descriptions", "Snapshots and Field overlays" (D-AGT-26), "Errors as guidance"; KLN "Storage, Git export and span provenance"; contract 7.6 "Free text is never endorsed by merging"
**Problem:** The handle rule covers source spans returned by `read.source`, `read.outline`, `read.docs` and `inspect.describe`, but a string literal written by a tainted agent becomes an ordinary runtime `String` once Kiln evaluates it: a part name, a BOM line description, a drawing note, a requirement statement, a check name, or text embossed into geometry. Those values reach clean sessions through `inspect.scene`, `read.bom`, `compare.diff`, CI reports, compiler diagnostics that quote source, and snapshots, all of which AGT declares non-tainting. Snapshots count as untrusted only when a Body "derives from an untrusted Asset", so an `emboss("…")` feature fed by an agent-written literal produces an instruction-capable image that every later vision call reads as trusted. This reopens R5-02's Critical channel one evaluation step later.
**Evidence:** ING: "`String`, `ExternalText` | Immutable NFC text; untrusted text from outside the design, written `external("…")` … never implicitly a `String`". Contract 6: `part(solid, name: "Bracket")`. AGT: "The scene graph, measurements and descriptions stay non-tainting, because they carry typed values and handles only." D-AGT-26: "A snapshot is untrusted and instruction-capable when the geometry or appearance of any visible Body derives from an untrusted Asset." KLN's node label is "the join of its inputs' labels"; span integrity is recorded in `repo` but no tab says it enters a Kiln label.
**Fix:** (1) ING: every value evaluated from a free-text span (string literal, description template, untrusted identifier) carries that span's integrity, and Kiln joins it into the integrity part of the node's label (R11-01). (2) AGT: every string-typed field in every method response (scene node names, item and BOM text, check and requirement names and statements, diagnostics quoting source, CI reports, diff text, description facts) whose producing node has untrusted integrity is returned as an `ExternalText` handle; state this in D-AGT-18 and in the method contracts. (3) Revise D-AGT-26: a snapshot or section SVG is instruction-capable when any visible Body, text, annotation or overlay derives from a node with untrusted integrity, from an Asset or from source. (4) Extend AGT-O-8 and ECO-O-18 with part names, BOM descriptions, drawing notes, diagnostics and embossed-text features written by a tainted context and merged by a human.

**Section:** Contract 7.8; KLN "Shared cache and remote evaluation" (D-KLN-9); ECO "Publishing and signing" (pipeline steps 2, 5 and 7); PLT "Tier 3 and servers", D-PLT-31
**Problem:** R5-03's fix trusts machines by what they run, but both trusted pools run third-party code. Tenant trusted builders evaluate merged revisions, which pull in third-party Wasm components and packages that no human reviewed when merging; PLT isolates those only as OS-sandboxed processes "one per (tenant, label set)" on hosts that may serve several tenants. The operator's registry builders run "std and public packages" (test vectors, acceptance checks) while holding "operator keys" and writing the global public domain. A sandbox escape is deterministic, so the same malicious package compromises every builder that runs it, and 2-of-n agreement then signs the poisoned value; two-builder agreement only defends against faults.
**Evidence:** KLN role table: "Operator registry builders | std and public packages | Operator keys | The global public domain, with 2-of-n agreement". ECO pipeline: "2. Rebuild hermetically … 5. Run domain acceptance checks contributed as data … 7. Run test vectors on every engine". PLT: "Trusted builders evaluate merged revisions of protected branches in one process per (tenant, label set)". Contract 7.8: "Release gates and every `SignOff` check accept a cached result only when two independent trusted builders produced the same `ObjectId`." D-ECO-26 justifies isolation by Wasmtime's 2026 escape-class advisories.
**Fix:** Amend contract 7.8: (1) Trusted builders and registry builders execute every Wasm component and package from outside std, `crucible::` and first-party translators only inside single-use microVMs, with the host computing output `ObjectId`s; OS-process sandboxes are not a trust boundary for attestation. (2) A node whose dependency closure contains third-party code is attested only into its tenant's domain, by builders dedicated to that tenant (no host shared across tenants). (3) The global public domain holds only results whose closure is first-party, produced by registry builders that never run third-party code; publish-time test vectors and acceptance checks for third-party packages run on untrusted-evaluation workers and never enter the global domain. (4) The hermetic builder for first-party packages, whose output runs inside the engine process, never builds third-party packages. (5) State that two-builder agreement protects against faults, not deterministic exploits. Add to KLN-O-TRUST-1 a planted package that escapes identically on every builder.

**Section:** Contract 7.6 "Context labels and write-down"; AGT "Context labels and write-down" (D-AGT-24), "Platform notes"; Open questions 10
**Problem:** For external hosts the model context is the OAuth token family, and "an external host gets a fresh label only through a fresh authorization grant". Crucible cannot see the host's conversation, so one conversation can hold two token families at once (two server entries for the same Crucible server) or re-authorize, and read under one label while writing under another, clean one. The most common desktop path, `crucible mcp` on stdio with the user's keychain credential, has no OAuth token family at all, so its context is undefined, and a relaunch of the stdio server is the natural candidate for a "fresh" context. Write-down and every integrity flag (and with them risk classes and auto-merge eligibility) can therefore be reset by the host.
**Evidence:** Contract 7.6: "for external MCP hosts it is the OAuth token family (client instance plus user), shared by every session that family opens." AGT: "An external host gets a fresh label only through a fresh authorization grant." AGT Platform notes: "`crucible mcp` runs on stdio with the user's keychain credential". AGT open question 10 asks whether "one family per workspace" is right.
**Fix:** Amend contract 7.6 and D-AGT-24: an external host's model context is (user, client identity), where client identity is the registered key of an attested client (D-AGT-19) and otherwise one shared "unattested" identity per user. Every token family, refresh, concurrent grant and stdio launch of that pair joins one monotone label, stored server-side. A label resets only through `session.reset_context`, which the human performs on the approval page with WebAuthn, attesting that the host conversation was cleared; the reset is audited and shown in provenance. Answer to AGT open question 10: one context per (user, client identity), not per workspace, because Crucible cannot observe host workspaces; the reset action is the escape hatch for accumulated flags. Add to AGT-O-17: two concurrent grants, a re-authorization and a stdio relaunch all keep the label.

**Section:** UIX "Approvals" (D-UIX-29); AGT "Acts and approvals" (D-AGT-20); PLT "OS services" (`Authenticator`)
**Problem:** The approval page is "rendered verbatim" by the desktop, web and tablet clients, but no tab isolates it from the rest of the client. In the web app it shares an origin with views that render untrusted content (imported names, SVG sections, Markdown descriptions, panel element trees), so a script injection there can fetch a pending approval challenge and start a WebAuthn ceremony under a pretext such as "confirm it's you"; the passkey prompt shows only the relying-party name, never the plan. On desktop, any UI code can call PLT's `Authenticator`.
**Evidence:** UIX D-UIX-29: "desktop, web and tablet clients render verbatim from the server's record". PLT: "`Authenticator` returns WebAuthn assertions with user verification for the approval page". No tab names an origin, relying-party id, content security policy or caller restriction for the approval ceremony.
**Fix:** Add to D-AGT-20 and D-UIX-29: the approval page is served from a dedicated origin (for example `approve.<deployment>`) with its own WebAuthn relying-party id, so credentials registered for the main app cannot approve; it renders only server-generated text under a strict CSP (`default-src 'none'`, scripts by hash); approval challenges are issued only to that origin (`SameSite=Strict` cookies, no CORS). The challenge is the hash of (plan digest, request id, approver id). Desktop and tablet clients open this origin in an isolated webview or the system browser; PLT's `Authenticator` is callable only from that view. Extend UIX-O-APPR-1 with a scripted main-origin page that tries to complete an approval.

**Section:** Contract 7.6 "Act approvals", 9 Tier 2; AGT D-AGT-20; UIX "Approvals"; KLN "Electronic signatures"
**Problem:** "No Act of any risk class is approvable on a phone" has no enforcement mechanism: WebAuthn does not reveal the device class, user-agent strings are client-controlled, and synced passkeys created on a phone are usable on any device. Synced passkeys are also exportable keys, which NIST SP 800-63B-4 bars from AAL3, yet they would sign export-officer declassifications, R4 Act approvals and Part 11 signatures. UIX-O-APPR-1's "phones … are refused" is therefore not machine-checkable as specified.
**Evidence:** NIST SP 800-63B-4: "syncable authenticators SHALL NOT be used at AAL3" and AAL3 requires "a cryptographic authenticator with a non-exportable private key" (https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html). UIX: "phone: 'approve on a desktop or tablet'". KLN signs with "ECDSA P-256 keys in platform keystores or WebAuthn authenticators".
**Fix:** Replace the phone rule with an enrolment rule in contract 7.6: approvals and signatures need a device-bound (non-exportable) credential registered through an enrolment that records device class, from a Crucible desktop or tablet app (which reports its form factor through the platform API) or a roaming security key whose attested AAGUID is on an allowlist. Synced passkeys may sign in but never approve or sign. Export-officer actions, R4-class Acts and Part 11 signatures require AAL3. KLN's signature record stores `authenticatorData`, `clientDataJSON` (challenge = the signed `ObjectId`) and the credential's attestation, so the record verifies offline. UIX-O-APPR-1 then tests "credential not enrolled for approval" instead of "phone".

**Section:** MFG "Approval, transfer and physical safety" (D-MFG-24), "Factory connection and digital twin" (D-MFG-20); AGT D-AGT-31
**Problem:** The gateway checks a short content hash that the post writes into the program header, which detects corruption but not substitution: a compromised server, relay or account can send any program with a self-consistent header, and the gateway never verifies that an assigned human approved that program. The approval therefore ends at the server, not at the machine. No tab states OPC UA security mode or certificate trust for the gateway's sessions.
**Evidence:** D-MFG-24: "Posts write item, revision, release id and a short content hash into the program header, and the gateway recomputes the hash on transfer and on read-back." D-AGT-31 makes approval "of the exact plan" the safety control. MFG has no occurrence of an OPC UA security policy or IEC 62443.
**Fix:** Add to D-MFG-24: the gateway transfers only a program whose full SHA-256 appears in an `ActionPlan` carrying a valid Approval assertion from a principal in the gateway's locally pinned approver set (a signed directory plus a transparency-log checkpoint), verified on the gateway itself; the short header hash stays only for operator display. OPC UA sessions use `SignAndEncrypt` with application certificates in a trust list managed by the site, and the gateway sits in an OT zone with one outbound conduit. Extend MFG-O-SAFE tests with a forged plan from a compromised server.

**Section:** Contract 2 External Op, 7.3, 7.8; KLN "Determinism policy"; ELX D-ELX-12, D-ELX-25
**Problem:** External Ops run only on untrusted-evaluation workers, but 7.8 lets release gates and `SignOff` checks accept a result only from two trusted builders, otherwise "they recompute", which for an External Op means another untrusted run. A `SignOff` check over an IBIS-AMI eye, an ngspice vendor-model run (ELX's default) or a GPL solver is therefore either never acceptable or silently exempt, and nothing binds the pinned result to the run that produced it: the guest computes its own outputs and no receipt is signed.
**Evidence:** Contract 7.8: "Release gates and every `SignOff` check accept a cached result only when two independent trusted builders produced the same `ObjectId` … otherwise they recompute." Contract 2: External Ops run "only on untrusted-evaluation workers". D-ELX-25: "Imported vendor models run by default in ngspice as an External Op". KLN: "External Op results | The host's class or `Unverified` | Only as `ObjectId`s the release pins".
**Fix:** Add an External Op rule to contract 7.8: a release gate or `SignOff` check accepts an External Op result when two single-use runs on different untrusted hosts produce the same output `ObjectId`, computed by each host outside the microVM and recorded in an execution receipt signed by a receipt key that never signs shared-cache attestations. Nondeterministic External Ops yield `Unverified` evidence that meets a gate only under a policy allowance, like a conditional `Pass`. KLN-O-TRUST-1 adds a forged guest output.

**Section:** Contract 7.8; PLT "Tier 3 and servers", "The compute runtime" (stdio MCP sandbox); ECO "Where translators run", "Tiers and contexts"; ELX "Engine choice"
**Problem:** Every native-code path receives labelled design data, and none states a network policy: External Op microVMs (vendor AMI libraries, emulators, vendor SPICE engines), the licensed-translator host, processes spawned through `crucible:tool/process`, and stdio MCP servers. Vendor engines also need licence servers, so egress cannot simply be absent. Untrusted native code with labelled inputs and an open socket is a direct exfiltration path that bypasses `release_data`.
**Evidence:** Contract 7.8 says untrusted workers "hold no attestation key and write only to a per-Proposal namespace", with no network rule. PLT: stdio MCP servers run "with only their pipes and user-granted folders". ECO's tool context imports `crucible:tool/process`. D-ELX-25 runs encrypted models "in their vendor's engine … where the user holds a licence".
**Fix:** Add to contract 7.8: every External Op host, translator host, spawned tool process and stdio MCP server runs with network egress denied by default; a manifest may declare named egress endpoints (a licence server, an MCP server's API host), which an administrator grants per organization and which the sandbox enforces by address, never by DNS name alone. A host with any egress grant may receive only inputs whose confidentiality label is at most `internal` and carries no `controls`, unless a two-person grant (D-AGT-27) names that host and label. PLT-O-WASM-6 and ECO-O-8 add a native guest that tries DNS, TCP, UDP and HTTP egress.

**Section:** KLN "Shared cache and remote evaluation", "Audit and encryption", "Phasing" (phase 1); contract 13.2 phase 1 scope
**Problem:** Phase 1's single-node team server is the only trusted builder and also runs microVM Proposal CI "on its host", while it holds the release-tag key, the signed audit log and the attestation role. Contract 7.8's separation of pools collapses onto one machine for the whole wedge, so one microVM escape reaches every key, exactly R5-03's failure. Firecracker also needs KVM, which a team server inside a cloud VM may lack.
**Evidence:** KLN: "In phase 1 the single-node team server is the only trusted builder, so release gates and `SignOff` checks recompute, and Proposal CI runs in microVMs on its host." KLN phase 1 includes "the release Act over approval subjects" and "a signed append-only audit log".
**Fix:** Add a phase 1 deployment rule to KLN: signing keys (release tags, audit log, attestation) live in a TPM, HSM or OS keystore whose signing service accepts requests only from the trusted-builder process over an authenticated local channel, never from the CI coordinator; Proposal CI uses Firecracker where KVM is present and gVisor otherwise, chosen and reported by the preflight check; External Ops are not offered on a single-node server; and every release on a single-node server records "single host" in its provenance. KLN-O-DEPLOY-2 adds a microVM-escape tabletop test showing which keys remain unreachable.

**Section:** ECO "Isolation and platforms" (D-ECO-10); PLT "Isolation of third-party Wasm components" (D-PLT-31), "Isolation and sign-in"
**Problem:** The browser sandbox for third-party Wasm components is "an opaque-origin sandboxed worker with no OPFS, cookies or credentials", but an opaque origin can still `fetch` any URL and send data in the request, since CORS restricts reading responses, not sending. The sandbox exists for the case where the Wasm sandbox fails, and in that case the worker holds the call's labelled inputs and an open network. The mechanism is also unspecified: workers have no `sandbox` attribute, so it must be a sandboxed iframe, which needs its own cross-origin-isolation headers to use threads.
**Evidence:** D-ECO-10: "Third-party Wasm components run in a separate opaque-origin sandboxed worker with no OPFS, cookies or credentials, exchanging data by `postMessage`". D-PLT-31: "a worker inside an opaque-origin sandboxed iframe without OPFS, cookies or keys". Neither mentions network.
**Fix:** Amend D-PLT-31 and D-ECO-10: the sandbox is an `<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts">` loaded from a dedicated sandbox site (a different registrable domain, so browsers place it in a separate process), whose document and worker scripts are served with `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'none'; script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'` (which blocks `fetch`, WebSocket and `importScripts`), `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp` and `Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy`. Data cross by transferable `ArrayBuffer`s. ECO-O-8 adds a red-team component that, given JavaScript execution in the worker, tries `fetch`, WebSocket, `importScripts` and navigation.

**Section:** "Risk classification" (D-AGT-16), "Auto-merge" (D-AGT-17), "Independent verifier", "Quarantined extraction and external hosts" (D-AGT-25)
**Problem:** R1 and auto-merge require "every authoring context clean", but for an external host Crucible sees only what it returned itself; the host's model may have read a poisoned web page, a local file or another MCP server's output before calling Crucible. "Clean" therefore means "clean as far as Crucible saw", which the tab presents as a property of the context. The same blind spot makes phase 1 verifier independence a claim about server session lineage only: one host conversation can run both the author and the "fresh" verifier under two agent principals of the same human. `allow_raw_external` "records the host's tool inventory", which the host self-reports.
**Evidence:** AGT risk table, R1: "every authoring context clean". D-AGT-17: auto-merge "only to R0 and R1 Proposals whose authoring contexts were all free of `instruction_tainted` and `data_untrusted`". "In phase 1 it runs in any MCP host under its own principal, and the server checks the lineage."
**Fix:** Revise D-AGT-16 and D-AGT-17: a context whose endpoint is `Declared` (any external host outside the model gateway) starts with `data_untrusted` set, so its Proposals are at least R2 and never auto-merge; only hosted-crew and gateway-attested contexts can be clean. A verifier review counts toward merge only when the verifier's delegating human differs from the author's, or the verifier runs in the hosted crew. D-AGT-25 records the host's declared tool inventory as `Declared`. Extend AGT-O-14 with an external-host Proposal that must classify as R2.

**Section:** ECO "Untrusted content in imported files"; AGT "Context labels and write-down", "Risk classification"; contract 7.6 "Free text is never endorsed by merging"
**Problem:** ECO's readers attach `data_untrusted` to every output of an imported Asset and Kiln joins it into everything derived, so any assembly containing one supplier STEP file taints every mass property, interference check and BOM line computed from it, forever. Contract 7.6 says a human merge endorses typed values, but that endorsement never reaches an Asset's label, so there is no way to say "this supplier geometry was reviewed". In practice every agent context working on a real assembly is `data_untrusted`, every Proposal is at least R2, and the risk classes stop discriminating.
**Evidence:** ECO: "Readers attach the Asset's `data_untrusted` integrity label to every output, and Kiln joins it into everything derived." AGT D-AGT-16: "any content from a `data_untrusted` context is at least R2". Contract 7.6: "A human merge endorses structure and typed values, never free text".
**Fix:** Add an Asset endorsement record to KLN and contract 7.6: a human who reviews an import Proposal (translation report, geometry overlay, `import_map`) signs an endorsement of the Asset's hash; from then on the Asset's typed outputs (geometry, structure, units, numbers) carry trusted integrity, while its text stays `ExternalText` and its renders follow R11-02. A new Asset revision starts untrusted again. AGT-O-14 adds a corpus case: an R1-shaped change on an assembly with an endorsed supplier part classifies as R1.

**Section:** KLN "Storage, Git export and span provenance", "Proposals and merge", "Sync, scale and recovery"; ECO "Exit surfaces"; AGT `edit.import_archive`
**Problem:** Span integrity is recorded "trusted when a person typed it", but content also enters a repository from outside the witnessing server: text edited in an exported Git repository and re-imported, a repository archive from another organization, a federated branch and an air-gapped bundle. None of these paths says what integrity the incoming spans get, and an archive or bundle carries the other side's own claims of "typed by a person". An agent-written injection can thus round-trip through Git or a partner's archive and return marked trusted.
**Evidence:** KLN: "Each source span records the integrity of the context that wrote it: trusted when a person typed it or the compiler produced it". KLN merge: "blocks match by block id, or by GumTree for files edited outside Crucible". KLN: "federation joins two organizations' servers through signed packages and shared branches"; `crucible bundle import` "verifies signatures, closure, labels and log consistency". AGT: `edit.import_archive` "ECO repository archive → a new design repository".
**Fix:** Add to KLN: integrity is asserted only by the server that witnessed the write. Spans arriving through Git import, archive import or federation get `data_untrusted`, and free-text spans among them `instruction_tainted`, unless the Change is signed by a device key of a principal in this organization; air-gapped bundles between sites of one organization keep integrity only when the signing site's key is in the receiving domain's trust list. KLN-O-SPAN-1 adds Git, archive and federation round trips of a planted comment.

**Section:** AGT "Write sets, protected paths and two-person rules" (D-AGT-27); KLN "Identity and authorization" (D-KLN-41)
**Problem:** Break-glass access "exists" with review afterwards, but neither tab bounds what it grants, who invokes it or for how long. If one administrator can break glass and then declassify, clear an endpoint or change a recipient, the two-person rule that fixed R5-15 is one click from void; if break-glass cannot do those things, the tabs do not say so.
**Evidence:** D-AGT-27: "break-glass access exists with a mandatory review afterwards and an alert to every administrator". D-KLN-41: "break-glass access alerts every administrator and requires review afterwards."
**Fix:** Specify break-glass in D-KLN-41: it is invoked by one administrator with an AAL3 credential (R11-06), lasts at most 4 hours, and grants only read access, agent freeze, ref revert, lock release and session termination. It can never declassify, clear an endpoint, client or recipient, change Cedar policy, purge, approve an Act or sign. Every action under it is audited with the break-glass id, and the review is a Proposal that a second administrator must close within 72 hours. KLN-O-POLICY-1 adds each forbidden action under break-glass.

**Section:** AGT "Audit and personal data"; KLN "Audit and encryption" (D-KLN-30)
**Problem:** AGT stores "full content only for Act plans, approvals and policy changes" in audit entries, while KLN says audit entries are "never labelled content". Act plans hold labelled file lists, recipient data and agent-written purposes. The entries live in per-tenant tlog-tiles logs whose data tiles are fetched by every verifying client and checkpoints are cosigned by customer witnesses, so labelled content in an entry reaches everyone who verifies the log.
**Evidence:** AGT: audit schema "with full content only for Act plans, approvals and policy changes". KLN: audit entries carry identifiers "never labelled content". D-KLN-30: logs "served in the C2SP tlog-tiles format, with checkpoints … optionally cosigned by customer witnesses."
**Fix:** One rule in KLN, cited by AGT: a log entry holds only identifiers, digests and the pseudonymous principal; the full Act plan, approval and policy text is a CAS record in the encryption domain of its label, and the entry commits to its `ObjectId`. Log readers who lack the label verify inclusion without reading content. KLN-O-AUDIT-1 adds a check that no tile holds labelled bytes.

**Section:** Contract 5 `ApprovalSubject`; KLN "Revisions and lifecycle states" (D-KLN-26), "Change orders" (D-KLN-28)
**Problem:** The approval subject is built from `ItemDefinition` `GeometryId`s with PMI, the check-verdict digest, effectivity and evidence ids. A `Software` item (firmware, bitstream) has no geometry, and neither the contract nor KLN says its binary digest is part of its definition. Because approvals deliberately ignore the `ChangeId`, a rebase that swaps a firmware binary while keeping geometry and check verdicts keeps every approval.
**Evidence:** Contract 5: `ApprovalSubject` is "{ base revisions, ItemDefinition GeometryIds with PMI attached by canonical entity number, check-verdict digest …, effectivity, evidence record ids }". KLN: an `ItemDefinition` "holds the `GeometryId`s of the Part or Assembly with PMI …, the `Material` version, properties, the BOM by value and documents by semantic content". Contract 2 defines Software items as BOM entries "bound to a programmable Instance".
**Fix:** Amend contract 5 and D-KLN-26: an `ItemDefinition` holds, per Item kind, everything that is manufactured or loaded: geometry and PMI for Parts and Assemblies; the binary `ObjectId`, its build provenance digest and the target binding for Software items; the posted program for `Program` items; the semantic content for documents. The approval subject covers the full released BOM by value with each line's definition digest. KLN-O-CHG-1 adds a firmware swap under an unchanged geometry that must void the approval.

**Section:** KLN "Items" (D-KLN-39); ECO "Enterprise connectors" (D-ECO-30)
**Problem:** In subordinate mode, "external approvals return as signed External inputs", signed by the connector rather than by a human principal. If they satisfy the release gate, an approval made in an external PLM (no WebAuthn, no assignment by Cedar, no Part 11 manifestation in Crucible, no binding to the plan page) replaces contract 7.6's approval controls, and anyone who can write the connector's input forges a release approval.
**Evidence:** D-KLN-39: "external approvals return as signed External inputs naming the Crucible approval subject". ECO: "External approvals return as signed External inputs naming the Crucible content digest, so approval still binds to content". Contract 2: an Approval is "A human principal's signature over the `ObjectId` of an approval subject".
**Fix:** State in D-KLN-39: an external approval is evidence, never an Approval. A release in subordinate mode still needs an Approval on Crucible's approval page by a principal Cedar assigns, which may be required to cite the matching external approval record; the external record is pinned in the release. Where the customer insists on the external system as the only approver, Crucible's release Act becomes `publish_to_system_of_record`, and the release record says "approved externally" with the external system named.

**Section:** AGT "Acts and approvals" (D-AGT-20, D-AGT-30); KLN "Data leaving a tenant" (D-KLN-40); ECO "Enterprise connectors" (D-ECO-30), "Exit surfaces"
**Problem:** Every byte leaving a tenant is a `release_data` Act, every Act needs a human Approval of its exact plan, and "standing pre-approvals" are rejected. Yet the same tabs route high-frequency flows through this family: each ERP item-master and BOM message, MES work-instruction pushes, each agent write to a branch shared with a supplier, and each Git mirror push. Either each needs a human approval (unworkable) or they bypass it (unstated). Human pushes to shared branches and federation sync are not covered at all.
**Evidence:** D-AGT-20 rejects "standing pre-approvals". D-ECO-30: "Outbound messages are `release_data` Acts". AGT: "Agent writes on branches shared with another organization need `act:share_external`". D-KLN-40 covers "agent writes to branches shared with another organization"; KLN's federation "joins two organizations' servers through signed packages and shared branches".
**Fix:** Add a `standing_release` Act class to D-AGT-30: one Approval, given under D-AGT-27 by two humans, fixes the recipient set, channel (connector id, shared branch, mirror URL), payload schema, confidentiality ceiling and expiry (at most 12 months). Each later transfer runs the `release_data` checks mechanically against it without a new approval, is audited, and appears in a weekly digest to the approvers; anything above the ceiling or outside the schema needs an ordinary Act. Human and agent pushes to shared branches and federation sync go through the same check. ECO-O-28 and KLN-O-RELEASE-1 add a standing release that refuses an over-ceiling payload.

**Section:** KLN "Data leaving a tenant" (`RecipientRecord`); AGT D-AGT-30
**Problem:** The `release_data` stage checks "labels against the recipient's attributes", but a `RecipientRecord` holds only "US-person status, country". Labels also carry organization `scopes` (customer, program) and `licences` (a supplier NDA model, licensed MMPDS values), and nothing in the recipient can satisfy or refuse them, so any verified recipient can receive any program's confidential data. AGT runs restricted-party screening at commit while KLN "reads … its screening result" stored on the record, so the two tabs disagree on whether screening is fresh; screening lists change daily.
**Evidence:** KLN: `RecipientRecord` holds "clearance attributes (US-person status, country) and expiry"; the stage "reads the labels, the `RecipientRecord`, its screening result". D-AGT-30: "restricted-party screening". The Consolidated Screening List combines Commerce, State and Treasury lists and "update[s] automatically every day" (https://www.trade.gov/consolidated-screening-list). COV D-COV-15 says export and release checks refuse what a licence forbids.
**Fix:** Give `RecipientRecord` a clearance: a bound on the confidentiality label (level, controls with their authorizations, scopes, licences), granted under D-AGT-27. `release_data` refuses any payload whose label exceeds it, and each `DataLicence` declares whether redistribution to a named third party is allowed. Screening runs at every commit against lists no older than 24 hours (the US Consolidated Screening List plus the EU and UK consolidated lists where the tenant's policy names them), and the record stores the list versions used. KLN-O-RELEASE-1 adds a scope mismatch, a licence mismatch and a party added to the list the day before.

**Section:** Contract 5 `Labels`; KLN "Labels and export control" (D-KLN-32), "Sync, scale and recovery"; AGT `ActionPlan.authorization`
**Problem:** The contract never defines what it means for a principal, endpoint or recipient to "satisfy" a `controls` element such as (EAR, 9E003) or (ITAR, XV). Deemed-export rules depend on the classification and the person's nationality, not on a US-person flag alone, and no record says who may grant access. `ActionPlan` cites an `ExportAuthorizationId` that no tab defines: who creates it, what it names and how it is checked. Nothing prevents a tenant from storing `controls`-labelled data in the standard cloud, where operator staff of any nationality can reach plaintext through KMS-backed envelope encryption.
**Evidence:** Contract 5: `controls` "is a set of (regime, classification) pairs such as (ITAR, category) or (EAR, ECCN)" and "A principal may read a value only if it satisfies every element." KLN attributes: "organization, US-person status, location, training, licences, clearances". AGT `ActionPlan`: `pub authorization: Option<ExportAuthorizationId>`. KLN: servers use "envelope encryption per domain under KMS or HSM keys".
**Fix:** Define in contract 5 a `ControlAuthorization` record [KLN]: regime, classification or category set, basis (US person, licence number, licence exception, no licence required), permitted countries and recipients, conditions and expiry, created by an `export_officer` with a second person (D-AGT-27). A principal, endpoint, recipient or service principal satisfies (regime, class) only through such a record; `ActionPlan.authorization` names one, and `release_data` checks recipient and controls against it. Placement default: a node whose label has non-empty `controls` runs and is stored only in the regulated cloud, end-to-end mode or a customer deployment, unless an authorization record covers the operator's staff. KLN-O-LABEL-1 adds a foreign-national principal reading (EAR, 9E003) without a record.

**Section:** AGT D-AGT-27; KLN D-KLN-41, "Shared cache and remote evaluation"; ECO D-ECO-26, D-ECO-28, D-ECO-29; PLT D-PLT-38
**Problem:** Enforcement predicates use `export_controlled`, a value from round 1's single data class that contract 5's lattice no longer has, so "dedicated VMs for `export_controlled` scopes", "registry refuses any package that carries `export_controlled` labels" and two-person clearing cannot be implemented as written. The two-person lists also differ: AGT includes clients but not purges, KLN includes purges but not clients.
**Evidence:** Six occurrences of `export_controlled` in KLN and ECO (for example D-ECO-29: "The registry refuses any package that carries `export_controlled` labels"). Contract 5's `level` is "public < internal < confidential" and `controls` is a set. D-AGT-27 lists "clearing an endpoint, client or recipient"; D-KLN-41 lists "clearing an endpoint or recipient … and purges".
**Fix:** Replace `export_controlled` everywhere by "a label with non-empty `controls`" and add the predicate `Labels::is_controlled()` to contract 5. Keep one two-person list, in D-KLN-41 (KLN owns policy records), including clients, purges, `ControlAuthorization` records (R11-21) and standing releases (R11-19); D-AGT-27 points to it.

**Section:** "Publishing and signing" (D-ECO-16); "Names and namespaces"
**Problem:** The namespace owner's offline key signs the trusted-publisher policy, but the delegation from the registry's targets role to that owner key must itself be signed, and ECO does not say by which key. If an online key signs new namespace delegations (as it must for namespaces to be claimable at any hour), a compromised registry re-delegates any namespace to its own key, and the claim "a compromised online registry key cannot add a publisher" fails. PEP 480, which ECO cites as its model, handles this with an offline-signed `claimed` role and an online `recently-claimed` role that administrators migrate periodically.
**Evidence:** ECO table: "Namespace policy | The owner's offline key signs the trusted publishers … as delegated TUF targets | Who may publish here"; "a compromised online registry key cannot add a publisher to a namespace with an offline policy". PEP 480: "The claimed role uses an offline key", "The recently-claimed role uses an online key", and administrators move projects to claimed periodically because they "have to use an offline key" (https://peps.python.org/pep-0480/). PEP 480 is still a Draft.
**Fix:** Add to D-ECO-16: namespace delegations live in an offline-signed `claimed` role, re-signed by the keyholders of D-ECO-22 at least weekly; a new namespace sits in an online-signed `recently-claimed` role until then, and clients warn on first resolution of a package from a recently-claimed namespace (existing lockfile signer pins still protect existing users). Owner-key rotation and loss recovery require the domain re-verification of the namespace rule plus a claimed-role re-signing. ECO-O-9 adds "online key re-delegates a claimed namespace".

**Section:** PLT "Build, release and CI" (D-PLT-40); ECO "Scanning, advisories and removal"
**Problem:** The engine process holds every open repository, token and device key, and it links the whole transitive crate graph. The only controls are cargo-deny (licences, known advisories, banned crates) and a risk register for "each core dependency". Nothing reviews the code of the hundreds of transitive crates, and build scripts and procedural macros run arbitrary code on developer machines and the hermetic builder at every build. A malicious update to a small transitive crate is the attack the registry tab defends third-party packages against, but not Crucible's own binary.
**Evidence:** PLT: "cargo-deny checks licences (no LGPL, GPL or AGPL linked), advisories and banned crates"; D-PLT-40 records "each core dependency's licence, risk class, owning engineer". cargo-vet's `safe-to-deploy` criterion certifies that a crate "will not introduce a serious security vulnerability to production software exposed to untrusted input" (https://mozilla.github.io/cargo-vet/built-in-criteria.html).
**Fix:** Add to D-PLT-40: every crate in the engine, UI, server and `wasm-host` dependency closure carries a cargo-vet `safe-to-deploy` audit, its own or imported from published audit sets the steward trusts, and CI fails on an unaudited crate or version delta; new crate versions wait 14 days unless they fix an advisory. Build scripts and procedural macros run inside the hermetic builder's sandbox with no network and a read-only source tree, and developer builds use the same sandbox by default.

**Section:** Contract 7.8; KLN "Electronic signatures" (D-KLN-42); PLT "Signed updates" (D-PLT-37); ECO "Publishing and signing"
**Problem:** The contract offers LMS "for release signing" beside ML-DSA-87 without the state-management rules a stateful scheme needs. SP 800-208 requires LMS keys to be generated and used only inside hardware modules that never export them and that persist the incremented leaf index before releasing each signature. HSM clusters that replicate keys for availability would then reuse one-time keys, which breaks the scheme. Per-tenant release tags and checkpoints are also high-volume signatures, a poor fit for a finite tree.
**Evidence:** Contract 7.8: "a classical signature plus ML-DSA-87, or LMS for release signing". NIST SP 800-208 section 8: implementations "shall only be validated for use within hardware cryptographic modules", "The cryptographic module shall not allow for the export of private keying material", and the module "shall increment the leaf index … and shall store the incremented leaf index value in nonvolatile storage before exporting a signature value" (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-208.pdf).
**Fix:** Amend contract 7.8: ML-DSA-87 is the post-quantum algorithm for every record. LMS (as HSS) is allowed only for the steward's software-release signing, with every bottom-level tree generated in its own HSM at a key ceremony, key replication disabled for LMS keys, and the remaining signature count monitored. Tenant release tags, checkpoints and provenance use ML-DSA-87 only. KLN-O-SIG-2 adds a cloned-state test that must be impossible by configuration.

**Section:** "Endpoint and client clearance" (D-AGT-19); Open questions 2
**Problem:** Open question 2 waits for counsel on whether a hosted endpoint can meet the ITAR end-to-end carve-out, but the carve-out cannot hold by construction: a hosted model decrypts prompts, and 22 CFR 120.54(b)(1)(ii) requires that "the means of decryption are not provided to any third party". The design needs a decision now so that phase 2's gateway and clearance records can be built.
**Evidence:** 22 CFR 120.54(a)(5) and (b)(1) as quoted at https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/22/120.54; AGT: "A hosted model provider decrypts prompts, so the third-party condition does not obviously hold for it".
**Fix:** Decide in D-AGT-19, answering open question 2: no endpoint operated by a third party is ever cleared for a label with non-empty `controls` on the basis of 120.54 or 15 CFR 734.18. Such labels are cleared only for endpoints inside the organization's own boundary, or inside a provider environment that the organization's export officer has authorized under a `ControlAuthorization` (R11-21), on the same basis as the regulated cloud (US persons, US regions); counsel reviews that authorization template once, not each endpoint.

**Section:** ECO "Marketplace" (Export row), "Security, export and trademarks" (D-ECO-29); KLN "Deployment"
**Problem:** Crucible's own products are CAD, CAM, PLM and BIM software, and both the EU and the US restrict exactly these to Russia and Belarus regardless of their export classification. ECO geo-restricts only "comprehensively sanctioned jurisdictions" for marketplace purchases, which Russia is not, and says nothing about the hosted service, commercial binaries, updates, support or licences. The EU ban also covers granting IP rights in such software, and its open-source carve-out exists only as a national authorisation.
**Evidence:** Regulation (EU) 833/2014 Article 5n(2b) prohibits providing "software for the management of enterprises, software for industrial design and manufacture … as listed in Annex XXXIX" to the Government of Russia or "legal persons, entities or bodies established in Russia"; Annex XXXIX lists ERP, PLM, BIM, CAD and CAM; paragraph 3a(c) covers licensing related IP; paragraph 9b allows authorisation "for the contribution of Russian nationals to international open-source projects" (consolidated text 20.07.2025, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02014R0833-20250720). 15 CFR 746.8(a)(8) requires a licence to export to or within Russia or Belarus ERP, PLM, BIM, CAD and CAM software designated EAR99, including updates (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/15/746.8).
**Fix:** Add to D-ECO-29 a sector-controls rule: tenants, marketplace buyers, support customers and update clients located in or established in Russia or Belarus are refused for the hosted service, commercial binaries, updates, licences, entitlements, certification and support; onboarding screens organizations for establishment and ownership; TUF update and registry servers geo-restrict those countries for commercial artifacts. Counsel decides, once, whether public open-source downloads need the Article 5n(9b) route. ECO-O-29 adds these cases, and the restricted-country list is a dated regulation package so changes are explicit.

**Section:** ECO "Security, export and trademarks", "Releases, editions and support"; PLT "Release channels and versions" (D-PLT-27)
**Problem:** ECO limits the company's CRA role to "its commercial distributions", but Recital 15 counts monetising through "a software platform through which the manufacturer monetises other services" as commercial activity, which describes the open core plus hosted service and marketplace; until the foundation transfer the company is likely the manufacturer of the open-source releases too. The CRA also requires a support period of at least five years, stated at purchase, while standard LTS lines last 24 months; Article 13(10) lets a manufacturer support only the latest version only if users can move to it free "and do not incur additional costs to adjust the hardware and software environment", which dropping an old macOS release on a 6-week train can break.
**Evidence:** Regulation (EU) 2024/2847 Recital 15; Article 13(8): "the support period shall be at least five years"; Article 13(10) and 13(19); Annex I Part II(2): "where technically feasible, new security updates shall be provided separately from functionality updates"; Article 71: the Regulation applies from 11 December 2027 and Article 14 from 11 September 2026 (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=OJ:L_202402847). Contract 9: macOS "current release and two prior".
**Fix:** In ECO, treat every distribution the company publishes (open-source releases included) as placed on the market by a manufacturer until the foundation transfer, with conformity assessment and technical documentation by 11 December 2027. Declare a CRA support period of at least five years for each stable release line: security fixes reach any release from the last five years either by backport or by a free upgrade path whose minimum OS and hardware requirements do not rise inside the period; the end date ships with each release. Security fixes on the train ship as separate patch releases (`x.y.z`) rather than only with the next feature release.

**Section:** "Scanning, advisories and removal" (Legal removal row); "Marketplace"
**Problem:** The registry stores and disseminates content provided by publishers to the public, so in the EU it is an online platform under the Digital Services Act, and the marketplace lets buyers conclude contracts with traders. The legal-removal row covers court orders, copyright and patent notices "after counter-notice where the law provides" but not the DSA's notice-and-action mechanism, statements of reasons to the affected publisher, internal complaint handling or trader traceability, and it names no US DMCA designated agent. The company exceeds the DSA's small-enterprise exemption at its planned headcount.
**Evidence:** Regulation (EU) 2022/2065: Article 3(i) defines an online platform as a hosting service that "stores and disseminates information to the public"; Article 16 requires hosting providers to let "any individual or entity" notify illegal content by electronic means; Article 17 requires "a clear and specific statement of reasons" for removals and restrictions; Article 19 exempts only micro and small enterprises; Article 30 requires trader traceability for platforms allowing consumers to conclude distance contracts (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32022R2065). Contract 13.2 puts headcount at 59 to 100 in phase 1.
**Fix:** Add a "Notices and moderation" rule to ECO: an electronic notice form (DSA Article 16) for any illegal-content claim, including export-controlled or sanctioned content; a statement of reasons to the publisher for every yank by operators, quarantine or removal (Article 17), recorded in the transparency log; an internal complaint path (Article 20); an annual transparency report; trader data collected from verified publishers before listing paid packages (Article 30, already partly met by know-your-business checks); and a registered DMCA agent with a repeat-infringer policy for the US. ECO-O-29 adds a notice-to-statement-of-reasons drill.

**Section:** MEC "Packages" (`std::standards::*`), "Part features" (thread, hole and fit tables); ECO "Licence and contributions" (D-ECO-20); ING fits
**Problem:** Phase 1 std ships "ISO, DIN, ASME, EN and AISC tables" (ISO 286 fits, ISO 261 and 965 threads, ASME B1.1, clearance holes; fastener dimensions in phase 2) inside std, which D-ECO-20 licenses under Apache-2.0. Standards bodies hold copyright in their publications and license machine-readable content only for use "without any modifications", and a substantial extraction of a tabular collection can infringe the EU sui generis database right. Crucible cannot grant Apache-2.0 rights in these tables, and the overview's "legal review of standards tables before phase 1" has no design to review.
**Evidence:** MEC: "`std::standards::*` | ISO, DIN, ASME, EN and AISC tables | 1"; `std::standards::iso286` and the thread packages in phase 1. D-ECO-20: Crucible's code including "std" is "licensed Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception". ISO's notice for its machine-readable files permits use "in their original format without any modifications" (https://standards.iso.org/iso/10303/). Directive 96/9/EC Article 7(1) protects against extraction "of the whole or of a substantial part" of a database (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:31996L0009).
**Fix:** Add a decision to MEC and a licence rule to ECO: std computes standard values from the formulas the standards define (ISO 286 tolerance grades and fundamental deviations, ISO 68-1 basic profiles), citing clause numbers, and ships no transcribed tables. Values that exist only as tables (fastener dimensions, AISC shapes, DIN legacy sizes) ship as separate `standards::` data packages carrying a `DataLicence`, obtained under a licence from the standards body or a licensed distributor, or supplied by the organization; they never enter Apache-2.0 std. Counsel reviews the formula approach before phase 1, as the overview requires.

**Section:** ECO "Mirrors, licences and the parts catalog" (D-ECO-18); ELX "Creating and migrating catalog parts"
**Problem:** Until a manufacturer verifies, "the operator curates" its `parts::` namespace, and ELX imports KiCad libraries "directly". Manufacturers' CAD models and datasheet compilations come under their own terms, often for design use without redistribution, and KiCad's libraries are CC-BY-SA 4.0, whose design exception does not cover redistributing library items as a collection. Republishing either in the public registry under Crucible's licence would infringe, and the registry's SPDX checks do not say which licences `parts::` data may carry.
**Evidence:** ECO: "A `parts::<manufacturer>` namespace belongs to the manufacturer once it verifies. Until then the operator curates it". ELX: "KiCad libraries import directly." KiCad's library licence: "Redistributed library collections must be shared under the same license agreement" (https://www.kicad.org/libraries/license/).
**Fix:** Add to D-ECO-18: operator-curated `parts::` packages contain only facts (dimensions, pin tables, ratings, each with its datasheet citation) and geometry that Crucible's own generators produce from those facts (ELX's footprint generators, MEC's parametric bodies); manufacturer CAD files enter only when the manufacturer's terms allow redistribution, recorded in `geometry_licence`. Migrated KiCad library items stay in organization-private packages, or in public packages licensed CC-BY-SA-4.0 with attribution kept. The registry refuses `parts::` packages whose data licence is missing or non-redistributable.

**Section:** "Strategy and exchange levels" (D-ECO-3); Open questions 3
**Problem:** STEP layer 1, on the phase 1 critical path, is generated from ISO's EXPRESS schemas, and open question 3 asks whether that is allowed. ISO's portal permits its machine-readable "electronic inserts" only "in their original format without any modifications for the purposes specified in their respective ISO standard(s)", under clauses of its customer licence. Vendoring the schemas in the open repository or relicensing generated code under Apache-2.0 is outside that permission.
**Evidence:** https://standards.iso.org/iso/10303/: "You are permitted to use the electronic insert(s) available on this site, in their original format without any modifications for the purposes specified in their respective ISO standard(s)", accepting "clauses 1. ISO's Copyright, 7. Termination, 8. Limitations, and 9. Governing Law."
**Fix:** Answer ECO open question 3: the repository never vendors ISO schema files; the generator fetches them by pinned hash at build time from the ISO portal (the purpose the standard specifies, implementing it), and the generated Rust contains only entity and attribute names and types, not schema text. Before month 6, the steward requests written permission from ISO through ISO/TC 184/SC 4 for distributing generated code under Apache-2.0; if refused, layer 1 ships as generated code built on users' machines from their own copy of the schemas. The `espr` decision stays as is.

**Section:** Contract 13.2 (phase 1 scope), 13.3 (rebuild rows); AGT "Benchmarking and training data"; ECO "Validation properties and corpora"; AGT Open questions 4; ECO Open questions 10
**Problem:** The contract makes an "ABC-derived 200-feature corpus" a performance gate and limits certified SSI to what "the prismatic ABC corpus" needs, while AGT excludes ABC "until per-document filtering is verified" and ECO uses it for "testing only". Copying the models for internal benchmarks is itself a use that needs a licence. Onshape's grant to the public depends on each document's owner plan, creation date and LICENSE tab, none of which the ABC download says per model.
**Evidence:** ABC: "The copyright of the CAD models is owned by their creators" and "For licensing details, see Onshape Terms of Use 1.g.ii" (https://deep-geometry.github.io/abc-dataset/). Onshape Terms of Use 1(g)(ii) grant a worldwide, royalty-free licence to "use, copy, modify, merge, publish, distribute, sublicense, and/or sell copies" for Free Plan users' public documents created on or after 7 August 2018 or without a LICENSE tab, while reserved rights in a LICENSE tab "will continue to apply" (https://www.onshape.com/en/legal/terms-of-use).
**Fix:** Answer AGT open question 4 and ECO open question 10: per-document filtering is reliable only with per-document evidence. Build the contract 13.3 corpus from ABC documents for which the Onshape API shows a Free Plan owner, a creation date on or after 7 August 2018 and no LICENSE tab, recording that evidence per model, topped up from Crucible's procedural generator; models without evidence are not copied. The filtered set may be used for benchmarks and published measurements; training still follows D-AGT-22. Contract 13.3 names "the licence-filtered ABC subset".

**Section:** Contract 7.7 (Licensing); PLT "OS services" (`CryptoProvider`), "Build, release and CI"; KLN "Audit and encryption" (FIPS mode); UIX "Design system and onboarding"
**Problem:** The contract's linked-licence list (MIT, Apache-2.0, BSD, ISC, Zlib, Unicode-3.0) excludes licences the spec already depends on. The FIPS build of AWS-LC, PLT's and KLN's leading candidate for FIPS mode, carries the OpenSSL licence; `webpki-roots` (common with rustls) is CDLA-Permissive-2.0; UIX bundles Inter, JetBrains Mono and Noto under the SIL Open Font License; and Tier 1 Linux links glibc, which is LGPL, while 7.7 says LGPL code "is never linked".
**Evidence:** crates.io: `aws-lc-fips-sys` 0.14.2 is "ISC AND (Apache-2.0 OR ISC) AND OpenSSL"; `webpki-roots` 1.0.9 is "CDLA-Permissive-2.0". UIX: "Inter (SIL Open Font License 1.1) … JetBrains Mono (OFL 1.1)". Contract 9: "glibc 2.34 or newer". Contract 7.7: "LGPL, GPL and AGPL code is never linked".
**Fix:** Amend contract 7.7: linked code may also use OpenSSL (the pre-3.0 dual licence), BSL-1.0, CC0-1.0, 0BSD and MIT-0; bundled data and fonts may use OFL-1.1, CDLA-Permissive-2.0, CC-BY-4.0 and Unicode-3.0, each with its notices; operating-system libraries (glibc, the C++ runtime under the GCC Runtime Library Exception, platform frameworks) are dynamically linked and never shipped, which LGPL permits. Every other licence needs an RFC. cargo-deny's allowlist (PLT) and ECO-O-31 follow this list.

**Section:** Contract 7.6 "Context labels and write-down"; AGT D-AGT-24
**Problem:** "Reading free text or images marks the context `instruction_tainted`" applies literally to trusted free text too: first-party std documentation, the delegating human's own comments and endorsed spans. Read as written, every context that calls `read.docs` becomes tainted, which contradicts D-AGT-18's three instruction sources.
**Evidence:** Contract 7.6: "Reading free text or images marks the context `instruction_tainted`; reading any untrusted value marks it `data_untrusted`." D-AGT-24 repeats it.
**Fix:** Reword contract 7.6 and D-AGT-24: "Reading untrusted free text (the content of an `ExternalText` handle) or an instruction-capable image (D-AGT-26) marks the context `instruction_tainted`."

**Section:** "Snapshots and Field overlays" (D-AGT-26); method catalog `inspect.ask_render`
**Problem:** `inspect.ask_render` lets a clean context query an untrusted image and get mark ids, booleans or counts, but the tab never says that these answers are untrusted values. They are computed by a model looking at attacker-controlled pixels, so they can steer the clean context's next edit.
**Evidence:** D-AGT-26: a clean context "asks about an untrusted snapshot only through `inspect.ask_render`, a quarantined vision call with a fixed template whose answers are mark ids, booleans or counts." The method table lists no label effect.
**Fix:** Add to D-AGT-26: `inspect.ask_render` answers are returned as `ValueRef`s and mark the context `data_untrusted`; templates come only from `std::agents` and are versioned with the role.

**Section:** AGT "Instruction authority and untrusted content" (D-AGT-18); KLN "Storage, Git export and span provenance"
**Problem:** An endorsed span is returned raw to agents, so endorsement grants instruction authority, yet D-AGT-18 lists only three instruction sources. Any human with edit rights can endorse, including the human who delegated the agent that wrote the span, so a phished low-privilege account can promote an injection.
**Evidence:** D-AGT-18: "Instruction authority comes from three sources only". AGT: "A span becomes trusted only through `propose.endorse_text`, a human action". The method table requires only `auth.human_only`.
**Fix:** Add endorsed spans to D-AGT-18 as a fourth source, scoped to the repository where they were endorsed. `propose.endorse_text` requires the `maintainer` or `approver` role, refuses the span's author and everyone in the authoring delegation chain, and writes a KLN signature record naming the span bytes.

**Section:** AGT "Acts and approvals"; KLN "Electronic signatures"
**Problem:** Both tabs make "an R4 Act" or "the highest Act risk class" a signature-record trigger, but risk classes R0 to R4 belong to Proposals; no tab gives Acts a risk class.
**Evidence:** AGT: "Every approval of a release or an R4 Act becomes a KLN signature record". KLN: "Every Approval of a release or of the highest Act risk class is a signature record".
**Fix:** Replace both phrases with "every Approval of a release, a data-release Act, a physical-effect Act or a standing release" (R11-19), which is the set the R5-21 fix needed.

**Section:** ECO "Events and webhooks" (D-ECO-12); KLN "Encryption at rest"
**Problem:** SSRF protection checks that a URL "must not resolve to" private ranges, which DNS rebinding defeats unless the address is checked at connect time, and redirects are not addressed. Thin payloads carry "hashes", yet KLN promises that "plaintext `ObjectId`s never leave the domain's principals"; the `ObjectId` of a small record (a parameter file, a lockfile entry) lets a receiver confirm a guessed value.
**Evidence:** ECO: "URLs must use HTTPS and must not resolve to loopback, link-local or private ranges". The Standard Webhooks specification recommends "a filtering proxy" that blocks internal addresses and treats any 3xx response as a failed delivery (https://github.com/standard-webhooks/standard-webhooks/blob/main/spec/standard-webhooks.md). KLN: "plaintext `ObjectId`s never leave the domain's principals".
**Fix:** Deliveries go through an egress proxy that checks each resolved address at connect time against loopback, private, link-local, CGNAT (100.64.0.0/10), IPv6 unique-local and IPv4-mapped ranges, and 3xx responses count as failures. For labels above `internal`, payloads carry per-subscription opaque ids (HMAC of the `ObjectId` under the subscription's key) instead of `ObjectId`s or file hashes.

**Section:** ECO "Names and namespaces" (look-alikes and new versions row), D-ECO-17
**Problem:** "New versions resolve for others only after 72 h, as KLN's policy sets", but KLN has no such policy, and no exception exists for versions that fix a published advisory, so security fixes wait three days. D-ECO-17 then argues against an unpublish window because "a design can be released within hours of a dependency's publication", which the 72-hour hold contradicts.
**Evidence:** ECO row as quoted; no "72 h" rule in KLN; D-ECO-17's rationale.
**Fix:** ECO owns the hold: new versions resolve for other organizations after 72 h, except a version that fixes a published OSV advisory against its predecessor, which resolves at once with a flag. Rewrite D-ECO-17's rationale around pinned designs needing the bytes for decades.

**Section:** "Licence and contributions" (D-ECO-21)
**Problem:** The copyleft similarity scan runs only on "agent-authored diffs over 50 lines", so it misses undeclared tool use and snippets split across small commits, which are the cases that need it.
**Evidence:** D-ECO-21: "Agent-authored diffs over 50 lines run a code-similarity scan against known copyleft corpora".
**Fix:** Scan every contribution's added code, declared or not, with a threshold on matched tokens per file and cumulatively per contributor per week; a match blocks the merge until a maintainer clears or rewrites it.

**Section:** KLN "Identity and authorization" (D-KLN-43); AGT "Audit and personal data" (D-AGT-32)
**Problem:** Both decisions rest retention of names under Part 11 on GDPR Article 17(3), but 17(3)(b) covers only legal obligations under "Union or Member State law"; a US FDA retention duty is neither. For an EU data subject, a US-only retention duty has to rest on 17(3)(e) (legal claims) or on the customer's own assessment as controller, which the design does not record.
**Evidence:** GDPR Article 17(3)(b): "for compliance with a legal obligation which requires processing by Union or Member State law"; 17(3)(e): "for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims" (https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/). D-KLN-43 treats "Part 11 retention" as a legal hold.
**Fix:** Add a `retention_basis` to each retention lock (`UnionOrMemberStateLaw { citation }`, `LegalClaims`, `ThirdCountryLaw { citation }`, `Contract`), set by the customer as controller. Erasure requests against a `ThirdCountryLaw` lock go to the customer's privacy officer instead of being refused automatically, and the DPIA template says so.

**Section:** Contract 13.1 Scope; KLN "Labels and export control"; AGT "Endpoint and client clearance"
**Problem:** Both carve-outs AGT and KLN rely on apply only to unclassified data, and the regulated cloud names ITAR and DFARS, but no tab says that national-security classified information is out of scope. Customers on defence programmes will ask, and the label lattice could be read as supporting it.
**Evidence:** 22 CFR 120.54(a)(5)(i) requires data to be "Unclassified" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/22/120.54). Contract 13.1's scope lists no exclusion.
**Fix:** Add to contract 13.1's "Out" list: "classified information under any national security classification system; no deployment mode is accredited for it". KLN's regulated-cloud row repeats it.

**Section:** "Physical tests and Evidence records" (D-KLN-35)
**Problem:** Evidence records are "signed with a TPM-held device key under measured boot", but no rule says how a runner is enrolled or how the server checks that the measured boot matches an approved runner image, so a runner with modified software signs records that look identical.
**Evidence:** D-KLN-35 and steps 1 to 6; KLN-O-HW-1 tests spoofed and replayed records but not a runner with altered firmware.
**Fix:** Specify enrolment: the runner proves its TPM endorsement-key chain, certifies an attestation key, and sends a quote over the boot PCRs with a server nonce; the server compares it against reference measurements signed by the runner image's build, and each Evidence record cites the quote. KLN-O-HW-1 adds a runner whose image differs from the reference.

**Section:** "SDKs, methods and the CLI"; "Security, export and trademarks"
**Problem:** ECO plans "PyPI as `crucible`", but that name is taken by an unrelated project, as is `crucible` on crates.io; the `[unverified]` note hides a decision. The trademark clearance cites only Atlassian, while another class 9 software product named Crucible existed (Amazon Game Studios' 2020 game).
**Evidence:** https://pypi.org/pypi/crucible/json returns version 0.7.0, a trading-signal measurement tool; https://crates.io/api/v1/crates/crucible returns an unrelated crate, while `crucible-sdk` returns 404. Wikipedia: Crucible was released on 20 May 2020 by Amazon Game Studios and its servers shut down on 9 November 2020 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crucible_(video_game)).
**Fix:** Add package-index names (PyPI, npm scope, crates.io, Maven, NuGet) to the phase 0 name gate in contract 13.1, reserved before any announcement; until the gate, ECO names the SDK `crucible-sdk` on every index. The clearance brief covers every class 9 and 42 use found, including lapsed product names.

**Section:** "Stewardship and decisions" (D-ECO-22); Open questions 5
**Problem:** "The trademarks are assigned in escrow to an independent party" while the company keeps using them. US law lets a mark be assigned only with its goodwill, and a mark whose owner exercises no control over its use risks losing significance as a mark; an escrow agent that owns the mark but controls nothing invites both problems.
**Evidence:** 15 U.S.C. 1060(a)(1): a registered mark is assignable "with the good will of the business" (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1060); 15 U.S.C. 1127 treats as abandoned a mark whose owner's course of conduct, "including acts of omission", causes it to lose its significance (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1127).
**Fix:** Replace escrow with an irrevocable, recorded option for the foundation to take assignment with goodwill at the trigger, secured by the steward's board and the keyholders of D-ECO-22, while the company keeps ownership and quality control until then. Answer to open question 5: join an existing open-source foundation that already holds trademarks and operates infrastructure for hosted projects, rather than create one, so that trademark holding, the CRA open-source steward role (Article 24) and registry operation have staff on day one.

**Section:** "Marketplace" (D-ECO-19); Open questions 6
**Problem:** Open question 6 leaves tax open, but EU VAT already decides it: a platform that authorises the charge or sets the general terms is treated as the supplier of electronically supplied services sold through it, whatever the contracts say. The marketplace does both.
**Evidence:** Implementing Regulation (EU) 282/2011 Article 9a(1), inserted by Regulation (EU) 1042/2013: a taxable person who "authorises the charge to the customer or the delivery of the services, or sets the general terms and conditions of the supply, shall not be permitted to explicitly indicate another person as the supplier" (https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32013R1042).
**Fix:** Answer open question 6 for tax: the steward company is the merchant of record for paid packages; the publisher agreement is a sale to the company, which invoices buyers and collects VAT and sales tax per buyer jurisdiction. Fees, refunds and disputes then follow the company's terms with buyers.

**Section:** Open questions 1, 7, 9 and 11
**Problem:** Four open questions in AGT's security area have no proposed answer, and each blocks a phase 2 contract (the gateway, extraction, budgets, cross-organization work).
**Evidence:** AGT open questions 1 (provider receipts), 7 (quarantine from another provider), 9 (host-declared tokens) and 11 (A2A 1.0 or shared Proposals).
**Fix:** (1) No provider receipts: hosts outside the gateway stay `Declared` until a provider publishes signed per-call receipts. (7) The quarantined model need not come from another provider; independence comes from context isolation (no tools, no shared context, schema-validated output), while a second provider adds a sub-processor for labelled data. It runs under a separate API project with retention off. (9) Budgets never enforce host-declared tokens; usage records them as `Declared` beside measured usage. (11) Agents work across organizations only through shared Proposals under `share_external` and standing releases (R11-19), never A2A, whose messages are free text outside labels, provenance and D-AGT-14.

**Section:** ECO Open questions 4, 7 and 9; KLN Open questions 7
**Problem:** Further open questions in ECO's and KLN's security and legal area have no proposed answers, although each is now decidable.
**Evidence:** The OSV schema adds an ecosystem when its owner sends a pull request, and the current schema is 1.9.1 (https://ossf.github.io/osv-schema/). ECO cites KiCad 9's open-source ODB++ writer as a differential oracle, showing that an open writer can exist.
**Fix:** ECO 4: send the pull request registering a `Crucible` ecosystem in phase 1, and publish correctness advisories in the same OSV database with a `database_specific.kind = "correctness"` field. ECO 7: counsel reads the ODB++ partnership terms before the phase 3 writer starts; if they forbid Apache-2.0 distribution, the writer ships as an external tool. ECO 9: use the code host's advisory identifiers plus OSV ids until the security team exists in phase 2, then apply for CNA scope covering Crucible's own products [unverified: CNA requirements not opened]. KLN 7: yes, a customer-hosted cache tier inside the end-to-end boundary, keyed in the customer's domain and trusted only by that customer's builders.
