**Section:** CONTRACT 7.4 Wasm execution; PLT Wasm component runtime (D-PLT-31, D-PLT-36); PLT The browser target
**Problem:** Contract 7.4 makes evaluation worlds synchronous and lets them import `crucible:ops`, and CCR-ECO-8 and CCR-PLT-5 (round 2) move every third-party Wasm component into an opaque-origin sandboxed iframe's worker that exchanges data with the engine by `postMessage` only. A synchronous import cannot be answered by a message that arrives on the caller's own blocked event loop, the sandbox cannot share a `SharedArrayBuffer` with the engine worker because it lives in another agent cluster, and PLT rules out JS Promise Integration. As specified, nesting, CAM strategies, slicers, placers and routers that call Anvil or Flux operations cannot run in a Tier 1 browser at all.
**Evidence:** Contract 7.4: "Evaluation worlds are synchronous and import no WASI; they may import `crucible:ops`." D-PLT-31: in browsers a third-party Wasm component "runs in a worker inside an opaque-origin sandboxed iframe without OPFS, cookies or keys, exchanging data by `postMessage`". PLT: "Relaxed SIMD, memory64, exception handling and JS Promise Integration are not used." HTML StructuredDeserialize for `SharedArrayBuffer`: "If targetRealm's corresponding agent cluster is not serialized.[[AgentCluster]], then throw a DataCloneError DOMException" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/structured-data.html); an opaque origin is its own site, so its workers form a separate cluster. A relay through the iframe's own main thread would need the sandboxed iframe to be cross-origin isolated, which no tab specifies. PLT's overhead table covers determinizer cost only, not the out-of-process call cost that round 2 introduced. WASI 0.3.0 (11 June 2026) made "async ... native to WebAssembly Components" (https://github.com/WebAssembly/WASI/releases).
**Fix:**
1. Contract 7.4: replace "Evaluation worlds are synchronous" with "Evaluation worlds import no WASI and are deterministic. Their `crucible:ops` imports are Component Model async functions in the callback ABI (no stack switching), so a host may answer them across a process or agent-cluster boundary; results never depend on completion order or timing, and fuel never counts host time." ECO regenerates the `crucible:ops` bindings; the browser first-party runtime (D-PLT-36) implements the callback ABI; native hosts may still answer synchronously.
2. Until the bridge passes PLT-O-WASM-1 in browsers, browsers evaluate third-party evaluation-world Wasm components remotely on the team server or a cloud worker, which contract 9's parity rule allows ("whether computed locally or through remote evaluation"). This also takes the browser sandbox out of phase 1, where the only third-party components are a user's own unpublished ones.
3. PLT adds rows to its overhead table, labelled targets: one `crucible:ops` round trip at most 20 µs between native processes and at most 250 µs across browser agent clusters, plus argument transfer per MiB. New oracle PLT-O-WASM-7: a reference component making 10,000 `anvil::offset` calls through each executor gives identical results and meets the rows.

**Section:** CONTRACT 1 Mission, 3 principle 6, 13.2 Program plan; Oracles in every tab
**Problem:** The mission and the 1.5× factor rest on swarms "working against oracles", yet every oracle sits in a directory agents cannot write, so each one, with its corpus and executable pass criterion, must be written and reviewed by people before any swarm work on its capability can start. Phase 0 and 1 capability rows cite about 427 distinct oracle ids, many on corpora that do not exist yet, while "oracles, corpora and QA" grows from 2 to 5 people and no milestone says when any oracle must exist. The spec has no build-program section at all: no work-item format, eligibility rule, runner class or review path for swarm output, and contract 13.2 lists "test corpora" as swarm work although agents cannot write `oracles/`.
**Evidence:** Parsing every capability table (Capability · Contract · Failure · Oracle id · Phase) gives 760 distinct cited oracle ids, 427 of them on rows phased 0 or 1. PLT: "All PLT oracles live in `oracles/plt/`, readable but not writable by agents"; UIX: "Oracles live in `oracles/uix/`, protected from agent edits." Corpora still to build include the "ABC-derived 200-feature corpus" and "a named GP1-class benchmark" (contract 13.3), "the prismatic ABC corpus" (13.2) and FLX's calibration entries with "at least 300 held-out samples and zero undershoots" per estimator class. Several oracles have runners agents cannot drive: PLT-O-PERF-1 on the physical reference laptop, UIX's "photodiode latency each phase", PLT-O-TGT-1's device farm, UIX-O-A11Y-3's screen readers and UIX-O-KEY-1's "reference tables kept by daily users". The only "swarm" text in the spec (AGT's Orchestration of swarms) describes agents using Crucible, not agents building it.
**Fix:** Add a "Build program" paragraph to contract 13.2, owned by PLT, which already owns engineering capacity:
1. **Oracle first.** An implementation work item opens only when its oracle ids exist in `oracles/` as executable checks reviewed by a second engineer. Chain A and B oracles exist by month 9 and every phase 1 oracle by month 15; each gate reports oracle coverage per crate.
2. **Runner classes.** Every oracle declares one runner class: `cpu-ci`, `browser-ci`, `gpu-lab`, `device-farm`, `physical` or `human`. Only `cpu-ci` and `browser-ci` work is swarm-eligible.
3. **Corpora.** Swarm-built corpora and reference data enter `oracles/` only through a human-reviewed Proposal and must agree with an independent source (MPFR, Open CASCADE, lib3mf, MFEM or libCEED, CAx-IF data).
4. **Staff.** Oracles, corpora and QA grow 4 → 10 instead of 2 → 5, or each domain team's line in the staffing table carries 15% of its engineer-years for oracle authorship, stated explicitly.
5. **Work items.** A work item is `{ crate, capability row, oracle ids, held-out split, budget }`, run through AGT's Plan and Proposal machinery against Crucible's own repository, with the verifier role of D-AGT-12.

**Section:** CONTRACT 13.2 Program plan ("A scope addition above 5 engineer-years to an open phase needs the same approval as a gate change"); Phasing in PLT, KLN, AGT, UIX, FLX
**Problem:** The round 2 fixes added or moved into phases 0 and 1 a set of capabilities that the round 1 drafts and R6-01's 200 engineer-year baseline did not contain, totalling an estimated 20 to 30 engineer-years. Neither the staffing table nor the 160 engineer-years changed, and no approval is recorded, so the gate date silently absorbs the additions.
**Evidence:** Absent from the `round-1` text of KLN, AGT, UIX and PLT and present now with phase 0 or 1 (git comparison): the opaque-origin browser sandbox and OS sandboxes for third-party Wasm components on every target (PLT "Third-party isolation", phase 1); one first-party browser Wasm component runtime (D-PLT-36, phase 1); microVM Proposal CI on the team server (KLN phase 1); context labels and write-down (KLN and AGT phase 1); two-person rules (KLN phase 1); `release_data` with restricted-party screening (KLN phase 1); label-aware egress (PLT and UIX phase 1); the stdio MCP server sandbox (PLT phase 1); GPU known-answer tests and per-pipeline classes (PLT phase 1); the heavy worker and one engine per origin (PLT phase 1). Contract 13.4 also put Lanczos and LOBPCG and inherent strain in phase 1, and FLX phase 1 adds beam-lattice strut buckling. Estimate (±50%): sandboxes and browser runtime 5, microVM CI 2, labels and write-down 4, span provenance and endorsement 2, approval page, `release_data` and two-person rules 3, egress and stdio sandbox 1.5, GPU known-answer machinery 1.5, browser engine ownership and heavy worker 2, FLX additions 3 to 4.
**Fix:** Record a phase 1 re-baseline in contract 13.2: re-estimate each tab against v5 bottom-up, list every addition with its engineer-years, and either approve the increase (phase 1 at about 185 engineer-years, ending at 110 people) or defer to phase 2 the items no GP1 or GP2 step needs. Candidates: the browser third-party sandbox (replaced by remote evaluation, R12-01), two-person rules beyond releases, and `release_data` screening for recipients inside the organization.

**Section:** CONTRACT 13.2 Program plan (phase 2 row); ruling on R6-34 in section 15
**Problem:** Phase 2 is sized at about 240 engineer-years, but it inherits most of the work cut from phase 1 and adds GP3 and GP4's own scope. By the program's own baseline, the backlog alone exceeds the phase. The ruling that accepted R6-34's phase 2 size is therefore inconsistent with the ruling that accepted R6-01's cuts.
**Evidence:** R6-01: "phases 0 and 1 as specified need about 465 engineer-years ... after the cuts ... about 200", so about 265 engineer-years were deferred "to phase 2 or 1.x release trains" (contract 13.2), among them cloud SaaS, live documents, encryption domains, transparency logs, CAM and posts, the cluster-DAG renderer, the public registry, the hosted crew, the code generator and TUF deltas. Phase 2 then adds work no deferral covers: mortar contact, shells, beams, thermo-elasto-plasticity and multibody (FLX), general NURBS SSI, stage 2 blends and sheet-metal unfolding (ANV), gears, weldments and 3D variation (MEC), nesting, press brake and structure-scale weld distortion (MFG), and general availability of four preview targets. Estimate: 300 to 370 engineer-years against 240.
**Fix:** Add a deferral ledger to contract 13.2 that names each deferred item, its engineer-years and its target phase. Then either size phase 2 at about 330 engineer-years (30 months, 100 → 170 people), or move named items that neither GP3 nor GP4 needs to phase 3: multi-tenant cloud SaaS, encryption domains, witnessed transparency logs, the hosted crew with nine further roles and swarms, the TypeScript SDK and C ABI, the k-buffer and variant grid, and Flatpak, AppImage and telemetry. Phase 4 then lands near year 10.5, not year 10.

**Section:** CONTRACT 13.3 Performance targets; PLT Phasing; PLT Performance engineering; UIX Two pipelines, State of the art
**Problem:** The rows of contract 13.3 have no phase, yet PLT makes GP1 and GP2 meet "every contract section 13.3 row" in phase 1, and every missed row blocks beta promotion. Phase 1 ships one forward renderer that UIX itself calls CPU-bound beyond about 10,000 Instances, has no single-Part golden product that exercises the 100,000-Instance or 1,000-part assembly rows, and gets KLN's scale targets only in phase 4. UIX also sets GP2's implicit lattice display at 30 fps, under a 60 fps orbit row.
**Evidence:** PLT Phasing, phase 1: "GP1 and GP2 meet every contract section 13.3 row on the reference laptop"; PLT: "A row missed on the reference laptop blocks beta promotion"; benchmark files `scene.toml` and `assembly-1000.toml`. D-UIX-9 rejects "per-object draws everywhere (CPU-bound beyond about 10,000 Instances)", and D-UIX-24 makes phase 1 a forward renderer with per-Part discrete LOD. 13.3: G1 100,000 Instances at 60 fps, G3 10,000 Instances, and "Open a 1,000-part assembly from warm cache: 10 s, with a coarse view in 2 s", whose coarse-first path in UIX uses "Root pages", which arrive with cluster-DAG pages in phase 2. UIX State of the art: "30 fps at 1080p on G1 for GP2". KLN Phasing: "scale targets (100,000-Instance assemblies, cloud cells)" in phase 4.
**Fix:** Add a Phase column to contract 13.3. Cold and warm start, selection, orbit at 5M triangles, drag, rebuild, recertification, simulation update, input to photon, memory, installed size and CEED rows are phase 1. Scene capacity and the 1,000-part assembly row are phase 2, gated on GP3 and GP4 with the cluster-DAG renderer. The 1,000,000-Instance high-band figure is phase 4, with KLN's scale targets. Add a phase 1 row "orbit of implicit Bodies: 30 fps at 2.1 MP on G1 and G2", and declare phase 1 forward-renderer capacity per tier as measured targets that do not block beta.

**Section:** CONTRACT 13.3 (reference laptop); PLT Performance engineering (D-PLT-28, Measurement protocol)
**Problem:** The contract fixes a processor, not a laptop. The Core Ultra 7 258V runs between 8 W and 37 W at the manufacturer's discretion and mixes 4 performance cores with 4 low-power efficient cores, so sustained throughput depends on chassis, firmware and power mode. The measurement protocol fixes run counts and percentiles but no power source, OS power mode, thermal preconditioning, panel refresh rate, or Windows and Ubuntu builds. Beta-blocking rows measured on an unnamed chassis are not reproducible, and the 120 Hz input-to-photon row needs a 120 Hz panel that nothing guarantees.
**Evidence:** Intel's specification for the 258V: "Performance cores 4", "Low-power efficient cores 4", "Base power 17 W", "Peak turbo power 37 W", "Minimum assured power 8 W", "Instruction set extensions: SSE4.1, SSE4.2, AVX2" (https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/products/sku/240957/intel-core-ultra-7-processor-258v-12m-cache-up-to-4-80-ghz/specifications.html). PLT: "Rows run 30 times unless stated", with no other conditions. Contract 13.3: "Input to photon, p99: 50 ms at 60 Hz; 33 ms at 120 Hz".
**Fix:** In D-PLT-28 and contract 13.3, name the exact laptop model and SKU (chassis, panel and its refresh rate, BIOS version), buy three units (one per OS and a spare), and fix the conditions: AC power, one named OS power mode, sustained package power read and logged per run, 10 minutes of thermal soak, ambient 20 to 25 °C, and pinned Windows 11 build, Ubuntu release, kernel and GPU drivers. Before each benchmark session, a calibration workload must land within 3% of its recorded value, or the session is discarded. If the chosen chassis has a 60 Hz panel, the 120 Hz row is measured on the macOS mid machine and does not block beta.

**Section:** CONTRACT 7.5 Shared kernel IR; 13.2 Staffing and milestones
**Problem:** Kernel IR v0 must freeze at month 6, yet the three compiler engineers who build it are first hires in months 0 to 4. Its first real consumers, H¹ elements with CG (months 6 to 12) and Anvil's implicit tapes (phase 1), arrive only after the freeze. Freezing before any consumer exercises the IR forces either a breaking v1 inside phase 1 or a v0 that bends around its first defects. The same problem affects every month-3 and month-6 milestone, because the plan names the first hires but not the 20 people who are in seat at month 0.
**Evidence:** Contract 7.5: "IR v0 freezes at month 6 with only the constructs phases 0 and 1 need (element kernels with sum factorization, pointwise constitutive functions with forward-mode derivatives, implicit tapes)". 13.2: "First hires (months 0 to 4): ... three compiler engineers for the kernel IR"; milestones 6 to 12: "CPU kernel back ends; H¹ elements, CG and manufactured-solution tests". Other early milestones with the same dependency: `detmath` C build by month 3 (D-PLT-17), toolkit decision at month 3 (D-UIX-3), and Ingot parser, types and interpreter, predicates and topology by month 6.
**Fix:** In contract 7.5, freeze IR v0 at the month-12 phase 0 gate, after one H¹ elasticity kernel with sum factorization, one constitutive function with forward-mode derivatives and one implicit tape have compiled through both CPU back ends and passed their oracles. From month 6 the IR is additive-only, except for defects those three consumers find. In 13.2, list the seed team of 20 by role, with an owner in seat at month 0 for every month-3 and month-6 milestone; any milestone without one moves by the owner's hiring lag.

**Section:** UIX UI toolkit (D-UIX-3); UIX Open questions 1
**Problem:** The month-3 bake-off cannot discriminate between its options. It asks about two engineers, hired in months 0 to 4, to build three screens twice on four platforms in six weeks, judged partly by UIX-O-A11Y-1 on Chrome, which neither option can pass while AccessKit has no web adapter. Masonry paints through Vello, whose original renderer needs compute (UIX's own words), so it has no G3 path, and it names no web backend. The capability row then defaults a failed bake-off to the own toolkit, so the outcome is fixed in advance and the six weeks buy no information.
**Evidence:** D-UIX-3: "chooses between its own retained-mode GPU toolkit ... and Masonry at month 3 of phase 0, after a six-week bake-off; the own toolkit is the working choice"; "The bake-off builds three screens with both options on Windows, macOS, Linux and Chrome". Capability row: "Neither option passes: own toolkit with gaps named". UIX: "Vello's original renderer needs GPU compute". Masonry's README: "Imaging (by default Vello and wgpu for 2D graphics)", with backends listed only for winit and Android (https://github.com/linebender/xilem/tree/main/masonry). AccessKit lists a web adapter only as planned (https://github.com/AccessKit/accesskit).
**Fix:** Answers UIX open question 1. Decide the own toolkit now. Masonry fails two hard requirements, a non-compute paint path for G3 and a browser target, and closing both is the same work as the own toolkit's renderer. Spend the six weeks on a risk spike of the own toolkit's three hardest parts instead: a 1,000,000-row virtualized tree with an AccessKit tree on Windows, an IME field on Windows and in Chrome through EditContext, and a 50,000-line code panel at 8 ms keystroke-to-paint. If any part misses its oracle at month 3, re-plan the UIX staffing line, not the toolkit choice.

**Section:** CONTRACT 13.2 Critical path for phase 1; UIX Phasing; KLN Phasing
**Problem:** Contract 13.2 names only two chains, geometry (A) and physics and printing (B), yet UIX turns the phase 1 gate into "designed, toleranced, simulated, reviewed and released through the UI, entirely by keyboard", and a release needs the team server, the approval page with WebAuthn and the release Act. The UI chain runs from the month-3 toolkit decision through toolkit core, renderer, sketching, dialogs, drag preview, the drawing editor and keyboard completeness. The release chain needs a single-node server with Cedar, a signed audit log, microVM CI, `release_data` and the approval page. Neither chain has milestones, and the month-20 dry run cannot exercise "released in Crucible" if the release chain is not ready.
**Evidence:** Contract 13.2 lists Chain A and Chain B only; milestones put "team server; Propose and review" somewhere in months 12 to 24 and "keyboard-complete workflows, accessibility" in months 24 to 32. UIX Phasing, phase 1: "GP1 and GP2 designed, toleranced, simulated, reviewed and released through the UI, entirely by keyboard". KLN phase 1: "the release Act over approval subjects; `release_data` for STEP and 3MF exports". Contract 13.1 gate: GP1 "designed, toleranced, simulated and released in Crucible".
**Fix:** Add to contract 13.2:
1. **Chain C (interface):** toolkit decision (month 3) → toolkit core, forward renderer, picking (month 12) → feature dialogs, sketching, drag preview, sections, Field color (month 18) → drawing editor and review diffs (month 22) → keyboard-complete and accessibility oracles green (month 32).
2. **Chain D (release):** single-node team server with Cedar and the audit log (month 15) → microVM Proposal CI (month 17) → approval page with WebAuthn and the release and `release_data` Acts (month 19) → used end to end in the month-20 dry run.

Also state that the gate reads "released in Crucible" as satisfied through `api` and the CLI, so that a UI slip moves UIX's own target and not the gate.

**Section:** CONTRACT 7.1 Anvil, 13.1 phase 0 gate; ANV Open questions 2; ANV Phasing
**Problem:** SSI heads Chain A and is "a phase 1 release risk" until counsel's opinion arrives, but no date requires the opinion; the phase 0 gate requires only that reviews be "commissioned". An adverse opinion at month 30 would block the release at month 36 after all of Chain A is built. GP1's surface set (planes, quadrics, tori and stage 1 blend supports) needs no sampling stage, so a phase 1 path can avoid the claimed point-set comparison by design. The wider search that ANV says was never done ("other GPU geometry patents were not searched") also has no date.
**Evidence:** Contract 13.1 phase 0 gate: "freedom-to-operate reviews commissioned". ANV: the patent "claims intersection points formed from points of one surface within a threshold distance of the other; claims 1, 6 and 11 compare point sets, and claim 16 recites no GPU"; "until the opinion arrives, SSI itself is a phase 1 release risk". ANV Phasing, phase 1: "analytic and NURBS–analytic SSI and Booleans ... (months 6 to 12)". ANV open question 2: "other GPU geometry patents were not searched."
**Fix:** The phase 0 gate requires counsel's written opinion on claims 1, 6, 11 and 16 of US 12,229,885 B1 and any continuations by month 9, and a freedom-to-operate search covering the phase 1 code paths of Chains A and B (SSI, Booleans, blends, tessellation, implicit lattice meshing) by month 12. In phase 1, Anvil intersects GP1's surface set by closed-form plane, quadric and torus intersections and certified subdivision for NURBS–analytic pairs, with no sampling stage on CPU or GPU, and counsel confirms that this path avoids the claimed comparison. D-ANV-17's GPU sampling path moves to phase 2 behind the opinion.

**Section:** CONTRACT 13.1 (GP2), 13.2 Chain B, 13.4 (inherent strain, phase 1); MFG Additive (D-MFG-25); ECO 3MF row
**Problem:** GP2's process is not defined, and the tabs assume incompatible ones. Inherent-strain prediction (phase 1 via contract 13.4) is a metal powder-bed method that "needs per-machine calibration" from MFG's coupons, yet D-MFG-25's hand-off names three FFF slicers. Crucible must mark 3MF's Beam Lattice extension as required, and a consumer that does not support it must refuse the file, so GP2 prints only if the vendor's build software reads beam lattices. Chain B also omits the calibration build that inherent strain needs before GP2 can be predicted.
**Evidence:** Contract 13.1: GP2 is "printed from Crucible's 3MF with the printer vendor's slicer". MFG: "FLX owns inherent-strain layer activation and prediction, from MFG's calibration coupons. The method is layer-lumped, so it needs per-machine calibration"; MFG-O-AM-8: "metal PBF build of GP2 within 0.1 mm in phase 2". D-MFG-25: a 3MF build "that OrcaSlicer, Bambu Studio and PrusaSlicer read". ECO phase 1: "GP2: 3MF with beam lattice". 3MF Beam Lattice 1.2.0: producers "MUST mark the "b" extension as required" (https://github.com/3MFConsortium/spec_beamlattice/blob/master/3MF%20Beam%20Lattice%20Extension.md). 3MF Core: "Editors and manufacturing devices MUST NOT process this model-file if they do not support the required extensions" (https://github.com/3MFConsortium/spec_core/blob/master/3MF%20Core%20Specification.md).
**Fix:** In phase 0, fix GP2's process, alloy or polymer, machine, print bureau, the vendor's build-preparation software and the 3MF extensions that software accepts, and record them in contract 13.1.
- **Metal powder-bed fusion:** Chain B gains "calibration coupons printed and measured (month 16) → inherent-strain calibration (month 18)" before the month-20 dry run. If the vendor software lacks Beam Lattice, Crucible writes a mesh 3MF with a declared triangle budget beside the beam-lattice file. D-MFG-25 adds the metal build-preparation software.
- **Polymer FFF:** inherent strain leaves phase 1 through a contract 13.4 change, and GP2 uses a strut lattice exported as a mesh, since the named FFF slicers are not shown to read beam lattices.

**Section:** CONTRACT 13.2 Program plan (swarm factor)
**Problem:** The plan caps swarms at 1.5× on oracle-covered work but does not say whether the 40 and 160 engineer-years are human effort before or after that credit. It does not count the human review time that every agent Proposal consumes, and it says nothing of how or when the factor will be measured. The only controlled field study the reviewer found measured a slowdown for experienced developers on mature codebases, so an unmeasured factor inside the baseline is a schedule risk.
**Evidence:** Contract 13.2: "Agent swarms count as at most a 1.5× productivity factor, applied only to oracle-covered, well-specified work". METR's randomized study of 16 experienced developers on 246 issues found they "take 19% longer" with AI tools allowed, while believing they had been sped up by about 20%; METR notes the results are now out of date (https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study/). D-AGT-12 requires a verifier on every agent Proposal, and protected branches require human review.
**Fix:** State in contract 13.2 that the engineer-year figures are human effort with no swarm credit. Measure the factor in phase 0 on three oracle-covered work streams: `detmath` Rust ports against the C build, STEP entity codecs from the EXPRESS generator, and toolkit widgets against UIX-O-INT-1. Measure accepted Proposals per reviewer-hour, defect escape rate, and agent compute cost. From the phase 0 gate, credit capacity at the measured factor, capped at 1.5, only to work items that meet R12-02's eligibility rule. Budget reviewer time explicitly, as a stated number of reviewer-hours per accepted agent Proposal.

**Section:** CONTRACT 3 principle 6; Oracles in every tab
**Problem:** Agents read every oracle's inputs and pass criteria, and only Anvil keeps held-out data outside the agent-readable tree. Code written against fixed visible inputs can pass by special-casing them, which is the standard failure of optimizing against a fixed test set. PLT's benchmark files, UIX's recorded scripts and reference images, and most corpora in other tabs are fixed and readable, so "oracle-covered" work is not yet evidence of correct behaviour.
**Evidence:** ANV: "Held-out ABC and Thingi10K subsets, chosen by a fixed hash rule, stay outside the agent-readable tree." PLT: oracles "readable but not writable by agents"; benchmark files "live in `oracles/plt/bench/`". UIX-O-SNAP-2: "Mean ꟻLIP at most 0.01 against references per backend"; UIX-O-ELX-1 replays "ELX's recorded routing and placement sessions". No other tab's Oracles section names a held-out split.
**Fix:** Contract principle 6 adds: "Every oracle that agent-built code is judged against has a held-out split outside the agent-readable tree, chosen by a fixed hash rule, or a property generator seeded at CI time and never shown to agents. A pass on visible inputs with a failure on held-out inputs fails the oracle." PLT adds held-out variants of each 13.3 benchmark (perturbed GP1 parameters, a second ABC sample); a visible-to-held-out performance gap above 10% fails PLT-O-PERF-1.

**Section:** CONTRACT 7.4 Executors (iPadOS); PLT Tablets and phones (D-PLT-33); PLT Open questions 1 and 2; UIX Platform notes
**Problem:** The contract claims the iPadOS app "meets App Review guidelines ... 3.2.2(i) ... and 4.7" while registry packages are "never ... a browsable catalog". But guideline 4.7.4 requires "an index of software and metadata available in your app" with universal links, and 4.7.1 and 4.7.5 add reporting, blocking and age restriction, which no tab plans for. D-PLT-33's first form, a WKWebView worker beside native engine threads, also cannot answer the synchronous `crucible:ops` imports of Wasm running in WebKit (R12-01): it would need a relay from a separate WebKit process through a callback-based reply handler. UIX has already picked the second form, while PLT defers the choice to a phase 3 spike, so the tabs disagree.
**Evidence:** App Review Guidelines: 2.5.2 forbids apps to "download, install, or execute code which introduces or changes features or functionality of the app"; 4.7.4: "You must provide an index of software and metadata available in your app. It must include universal links that lead to all of the software offered in your app"; 3.2.2(i) bans an interface "similar to the App Store or as a general-interest collection" (https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/). Apple's `WKScriptMessageHandlerWithReply` answers JavaScript through a `replyHandler: (Any?, String?) -> Void` callback (https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/documentation/webkit/wkscriptmessagehandlerwithreply.json). UIX: "On iPadOS the web build runs in a thin WKWebView shell"; PLT open question 2: "A phase 3 spike ... picks one of D-PLT-33's two forms".
**Fix:** Answers PLT open questions 1 and 2.
1. iPadOS uses only the second form, the web build in a WKWebView shell, so it shares the browser runtime and the async `crucible:ops` bridge of R12-01.
2. Only first-party Wasm components shipped in the binary run locally. Registry Wasm components evaluate remotely by default, which keeps the app inside 2.5.2 and outside 4.7.
3. Replace the contract sentence with "the app runs only first-party Wasm components locally and evaluates registry Wasm components remotely". If local registry components are ever wanted, ECO first ships a 4.7.4 index on the web with universal links, 4.7.1 reporting and blocking through its legal-removal path, and a 4.7.5 age mechanism.
4. The phase 3 spike measures WKWebView memory limits and WebGPU only.

**Section:** PLT OS services (`Authenticator`), capability "WebAuthn"; UIX Approvals (D-UIX-29); AGT D-AGT-20
**Problem:** Every Act approval needs WebAuthn user verification, which PLT's `Authenticator` provides natively on each desktop. On Apple platforms an app can use passkeys only for relying parties listed as its associated domains, so the native macOS app cannot approve against a customer's self-hosted team server, the only server in phase 1. PLT names no Linux mechanism. Approvals on a general-availability Tier 1 target therefore fail for the phase 1 deployment model.
**Evidence:** Apple, Supporting passkeys: "You need to have an associated domain with the `webcredentials` service type when making a registration or assertion request; otherwise, the request returns an error"; "Your app can't use passkeys to authenticate for services that you haven't configured as the app's associated domains" (https://developer.apple.com/tutorials/data/documentation/authenticationservices/supporting-passkeys.json). PLT: "`Authenticator` returns WebAuthn assertions with user verification for the approval page"; capability "WebAuthn | `Authenticator` assertions with user verification | ... | 1". KLN phase 1: "a single-node team server".
**Fix:** Native desktop and tablet clients open the approval page in a browser session: `ASWebAuthenticationSession` on macOS and iPadOS, and the default browser on Windows and Linux, bound to the request id and returned to the app by a `crucible://` callback. The browser, not the app, performs WebAuthn, for any relying-party domain. `Authenticator` is used natively only where the relying party is an associated domain of the shipped app (Crucible's own cloud). PLT-O-OS-4 adds an approval against a self-hosted domain on every desktop OS.

**Section:** AGT Acts and approvals (D-AGT-20, D-AGT-30); KLN Phasing (`release_data` for STEP and 3MF exports); MFG D-MFG-25
**Problem:** Every byte that leaves a tenant goes through the `release_data` Act family, and every Act needs an assigned Approval on the server's page with WebAuthn. KLN applies this to STEP and 3MF exports in phase 1, and no tab says where the tenant boundary lies for a local file. So the phase 1 wedge user, who hands a 3MF to their own slicer (D-MFG-25) or saves a STEP file for a shop, needs a team server, an inbox, a passkey and a recipient record for each export. The spec does not define whether a desktop install without a server can export at all.
**Evidence:** D-AGT-30: "Every byte that leaves a tenant goes through one Act family, `release_data` ... restricted-party screening ... audit". D-AGT-20: "`act.commit` creates an approval request that Cedar policy assigns to named approvers ... after phishing-resistant WebAuthn user verification". KLN phase 1: "`release_data` for STEP and 3MF exports". D-MFG-25: Crucible "writes a 3MF build ... and opens it there". Contract 13.1 names phase 1 the "Wedge: code-CAD and 3D printing".
**Fix:** In D-AGT-30 and KLN, define the tenant boundary for local files. A human principal writing an export to a local folder or a local application is an audited local write, not an Act, when the payload's label is `public` or `internal`, carries no export control, and is not addressed to a recipient record. Agent-prepared exports, labelled or controlled payloads, and every transfer to another organization stay `release_data` Acts. State in contract 13.2 whether phase 1 supports a desktop install without a team server, and what it can do.

**Section:** CONTRACT 7.4 (determinizer cancellation); PLT D-PLT-9, The determinizer, PLT-O-WASM-3
**Problem:** Without cross-origin isolation the web build has no shared memory, so a cancellation sent from the UI is a message queued on the engine worker's event loop, which is blocked for as long as an Op runs. "Yields to the host every fixed number of fuel units" gives the host nothing to read, because the host import runs on the same blocked thread. The R3-21 fix therefore does not hold in the single-threaded build: drag previews, which Kiln cancels on every pointer move, run to completion there.
**Evidence:** Contract 7.4: fuel metering "with a check that also reads a host cancellation word, or yields to the host every fixed number of fuel units where shared memory is absent". PLT: "the unisolated build [passes `api` messages] through transferred buffers". D-PLT-9: the page loads "the single-threaded build" when `crossOriginIsolated` is false. PLT-O-WASM-3: "Cancellation lands at fuel checks everywhere".
**Fix:** Contract 7.4 replaces the clause with: "Where shared memory is absent, cancellation lands at Op boundaries; Kiln runs every Op estimated above 100 ms in a disposable worker and cancels it by terminating that worker." PLT-O-WASM-3 adds the unisolated build with a target of p99 cancel-to-idle within 150 ms, and the drag row states that it is measured on the threaded build.

**Section:** PLT Memory (D-PLT-30, browser memory table); PLT Open questions 3; CONTRACT 9 Browser memory, 13.3 Memory row
**Problem:** Only the heavy worker is ever terminated, while every evaluation estimated below 512 MiB runs in the engine worker. Its linear memory therefore sits at its session high-water mark, up to the 1.5 GiB cap. The table's "Idle, UI plus engine 300 MiB after a heavy-worker recycle" holds only for a session that never opened a design, the same session that held "GP1 open 1.5 GiB of linear memory in total". R6-14's fix does not hold for the engine worker.
**Evidence:** PLT: WebAssembly memory "can only grow and never shrink"; D-PLT-30: "every evaluation estimated above 512 MiB runs in a disposable heavy worker"; the memory table rows "Engine worker | 1.5 GiB linear memory", "Idle, UI plus engine | 300 MiB after a heavy-worker recycle", "GP1 open | 1.5 GiB of linear memory in total". PLT-O-WEB-3: "recycle restores idle memory".
**Fix:** The engine worker recycles too. When its linear memory exceeds 768 MiB and the session has been idle for 30 s, it hands the Web Lock to a fresh engine worker that replays the journal through D-PLT-29's takeover path, with memo tables already in OPFS. The idle row is measured after that recycle. Answer to PLT open question 3: set the caps per browser engine from the phase 0 kill-threshold measurements on the 8 GB low-band machine, which is the binding case, and publish them in the table as figures, not proposals.

**Section:** PLT The browser target (D-PLT-29, D-PLT-30)
**Problem:** D-PLT-29 makes the engine worker the owner of "every OPFS write handle (CAS packs, journal, ...)", while D-PLT-30's heavy worker "writes results to the OPFS CAS". Synchronous access handles lock per file, so the heavy worker cannot write those packs. The heavy worker also has no thread pool, because the wasm-bindgen-rayon compute workers share the engine module's memory, not the heavy worker's. Evaluations above 512 MiB, which include most `Interactive` and `SignOff` solves in browsers, therefore run single-threaded, or their pool start-up is uncounted.
**Evidence:** D-PLT-29: "The first tab's engine worker takes a Web Lock and owns every OPFS write handle"; PLT: a synchronous access handle "takes an exclusive lock on the file". D-PLT-30: the heavy worker "writes results to the OPFS CAS and terminates". The context table lists "Compute workers ... The compute pool through wasm-bindgen-rayon" beside "Heavy worker | One disposable evaluation with its own memory".
**Fix:**
1. The heavy worker writes a new pack file under a name only it holds, then sends the pack's index to the engine worker, which adopts it. D-PLT-29 then reads "every OPFS write handle except heavy-worker packs in transfer".
2. The heavy worker starts its own pool of min(`hardwareConcurrency` − 2, 8) nested workers on its own shared memory, the engine pauses its pool while a heavy evaluation runs, and Kiln's cost model includes pool start-up.
3. PLT-O-WEB-3 adds a heavy evaluation at 1 and 8 threads with identical hashes and the expected speed-up.

**Section:** KLN Deployment ("Team server | One container ... microVM CI"); PLT Tier 3 and servers; D-KLN-9
**Problem:** The phase 1 team server is "one container" that runs Proposal CI in Firecracker- or gVisor-class microVMs. Firecracker needs `/dev/kvm`, which ordinary cloud VMs and unprivileged containers do not expose, so the single-node server's sandbox works only on bare metal or with KVM passed through. The same host also runs the only trusted builder, and no tab states what separates the two pools on one machine.
**Evidence:** KLN: "Team server | One container: repository server, CI coordinator, microVM CI, optional workers". KLN: "In phase 1 the single-node team server is the only trusted builder ... and Proposal CI runs in microVMs on its host." Firecracker: "Firecracker requires read/write access to `/dev/kvm` exposed by the KVM module"; "EC2 only supports KVM on `.metal` instance types" (https://github.com/firecracker-microvm/firecracker/blob/main/docs/getting-started.md).
**Fix:** In KLN and PLT, the single-node team server becomes a host or VM install, not one container. It ships two untrusted-evaluation back ends: Firecracker where `/dev/kvm` exists, and gVisor otherwise. The installer reports which one is active, and the health check refuses Proposal CI when neither works. The trusted builder runs under a separate OS user with no access to the sandbox service's sockets or images. PLT-O-TGT-2 runs on a KVM host and on a cloud VM without nested virtualization.

**Section:** PLT Targets (Wasmtime tier text, capability "Upstream Wasmtime coverage"); CONTRACT 9 Tier 1 preview
**Problem:** PLT keeps Windows ARM64 in preview until upstream Wasmtime rates `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` Tier 2, which is a decision outside Crucible's control. Contract 9 allows a preview target "for at most one phase", so if upstream has not promoted the target by the phase 2 gate, the two rules conflict and parity breaks.
**Evidence:** PLT capability: "Upstream Wasmtime coverage | Fuzzing and CI funded for ARM64 and mobile targets | Below Tier 2: the target stays in preview". Wasmtime's tiers page rates aarch64 Windows Tier 3, needing "CI testing" and a "full-time maintainer" (https://docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-tiers.html). Contract 9: "A Tier 1 target may be a preview target for at most one phase".
**Fix:** Replace the upstream label with Crucible-owned criteria. Crucible's CI runs Wasmtime's own test suite and PLT-O-WASM-1 to PLT-O-WASM-6 on `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` on every merge, plus at least 24 hours of fuzzing a week; meeting both qualifies general availability whatever upstream's label. If they are not met by the phase 2 gate, Windows ARM64 runs Wasm components through Pulley, with its speed declared as capacity, and stays general-availability.

**Section:** CONTRACT 13.2 Staffing; PLT CI stages and capacity; PLT Release channels
**Problem:** "Build, release, CI, GPU lab and SRE" grows from 4 to 5 people, but by phase 1 they run about 3,000 cloud vCPUs, 72 macOS, ARM64 and lab machines, a GPU lab with pinned drivers and canary upgrades, a Tier 2 device farm, four package formats with HSM signing and TUF key ceremonies, reproducible builds for two targets, a 6-hour nightly suite with automatic bisection, and the team server's operations. The plan also has no non-labour budget, although continuous CI capacity at this scale costs on the order of USD 1 million a year (estimate) before lab hardware, physical runs, metrology and counsel.
**Evidence:** PLT: "phase 1 about 3,000, 24, 24 and 24" (cloud vCPUs; macOS runners; ARM64 runners; lab machines), "Each machine keeps a fixed driver, and upgrades pass a canary first", TUF root "3 of 5 offline hardware tokens held by separate people". Contract 13.2: "build, release, CI, GPU lab and SRE 4 → 5". Cost estimate: 3,000 vCPUs × 8,760 h × about USD 0.04 per vCPU-hour.
**Fix:** In contract 13.2, grow this line 4 → 9: CI and runners 2, GPU lab and device farm 2, release engineering and signing 2, reproducible builds 1, and SRE 2. Add a non-labour table per phase (±50%) covering cloud CI, runner and lab hardware, physical golden-product runs with replicates and re-runs, metrology, and counsel.

**Section:** CONTRACT 13.3 (Flux CPU throughput row); PLT D-PLT-18; PLT Open questions 4
**Problem:** The CEED row sets "at least 50% of MFEM or libCEED" for BP3 and BP5 at p ≥ 3, but it does not name the class it is measured in. Canonical kernels carry no FMA, while MFEM and libCEED use it, so in the canonical class the row demands MFEM's full efficiency against half the arithmetic peak. In a `CpuIsa` class with FMA, the row says nothing about the sign-off path.
**Evidence:** Contract 13.3 row; D-PLT-18: a kernel family that loses more than 1.3 times "may ship a `CpuIsa` variant with FMA for `Preview` and `Interactive` results; `SignOff` recomputes canonically". PLT open question 4: "Which kernel families ship `CpuIsa` variants".
**Fix:** Answers PLT open question 4. The row reads "in `CpuIsa { X86_64V3 }` with FMA, against MFEM and libCEED built for the same ISA on the reference laptop". A second row sets canonical-class targets of 30% for BP3 and BP5 at p ≥ 3 and 70% for BP1 and BP2. Sum factorization at p ≥ 3, dense GEMM and LU, and NURBS evaluation ship FMA variants from phase 0; other families only after measurement.

**Section:** CONTRACT 9 Tier 1 preview; PLT Targets; PLT The determinism suite
**Problem:** Three criteria of the preview rule cannot be executed as worded. Preview targets must pass "the golden-product checks headless", but Safari is a preview target and PLT names no runner that drives real Safari, and a WebKit build is not Safari. "Accessibility certification" is not a defined artefact for WCAG, which has conformance claims rather than certificates. "GPU-driver qualification" has no pass criterion.
**Evidence:** Contract 9: "runs the same build with identical features, passes the determinism suite and the golden-product checks headless ... installers, updater, accessibility certification and GPU-driver qualification complete by the next gate". The PLT suite names "wasm32 in Node and headless Chrome" for the per-merge set, and only "every other Tier 1 target and browser engine" nightly.
**Fix:**
- **Safari:** contract 9 reads "golden-product checks in automation", and PLT names a Safari runner (safaridriver on a logged-in macOS CI host).
- **Accessibility:** "accessibility certification" means a published Accessibility Conformance Report per target, built on UIX-O-A11Y-1 to UIX-O-A11Y-3 plus an external audit.
- **GPU drivers:** "GPU-driver qualification" means PLT-O-GPU-1 and UIX-O-SNAP-2 pass on every lab device listed for the target.

**Section:** CONTRACT 13.2 milestones (hardening months 24–32, physical runs 30–34, gate 36)
**Problem:** GP1 and GP2 are made in months 30 to 34 from outputs of a build that hardening keeps changing until month 32, so the release judged at month 36 is not the one whose STEP and 3MF files produced the measured articles. The gate does not say how the two are tied.
**Evidence:** Contract 13.2 milestones: "24–32 | Hardening ..."; "30–34 | GP1 and GP2 physical runs, with one re-run budgeted"; "36 | Phase 1 gate".
**Fix:** Contract 13.1 adds that the gate release must reproduce the run build's exported STEP AP242 and 3MF bit for bit (equal `ObjectId`s), or else show equal `GeometryId`s and PMI with a reviewed diff of non-geometric content. Otherwise the run repeats. The run build is tagged at month 29.

**Section:** AGT Phasing, phase 1
**Problem:** AGT's phase 1 gate contribution includes "pass^1 ≥ 80% and pass^4 ≥ 60% on the best qualified endpoint", measured through external MCP hosts and third-party models. Whether a phase gate passes should not depend on a vendor's model release.
**Evidence:** AGT Phasing, phase 1: "Golden tasks on GP1 and GP2 reach pass^1 ≥ 80% and pass^4 ≥ 60% on the best qualified endpoint (targets)".
**Fix:** The phase 1 gate contribution becomes "the golden-task harness, injection suite and qualification run on at least two endpoints and report pass^1 and pass^4". The thresholds govern which endpoints qualify for each role (AGT's endpoint qualification by golden tasks), not the phase gate.

**Section:** FLX `Interactive` stage budgets; FLX-O-MESH-3
**Problem:** FLX measures its `Interactive` stage budgets "on GP1, GP2 and GP5 in phase 0", but GP5, a molded enclosure with its PCB, is a phase 3 golden product whose design needs moulding features and board outlines that phase 0 does not have.
**Evidence:** FLX: "Stage budgets, measured on GP1, GP2 and GP5 in phase 0 (targets; Anvil owns the first two)"; FLX-O-MESH-3: "Each stage within budget on GP1, GP2 and GP5 benchmarks". Contract 13.1: GP5 closes phase 3.
**Fix:** Until phase 3, the third benchmark is a named thin-walled part from the ABC corpus with a stated wall-thickness range. GP5 replaces it at the phase 3 gate.

**Section:** UIX GPU capability tiers; UIX Platform notes (macOS)
**Problem:** The tier table makes 64-bit atomic min and max a G1 requirement, but compute rasterization, the only user, arrives in phase 2. The platform notes then let Apple GPUs without these atomics "run G1 without compute rasterization", which contradicts the table and leaves capacity undeclared for that case.
**Evidence:** UIX tier table, G1: "Compute, storage buffers, indirect draws; 64-bit atomic min and max for compute rasterization". UIX Platform notes: "some older Apple GPUs may lack 64-bit atomic min and max [unverified], so they run G1 without compute rasterization".
**Fix:** G1 requires native compute, storage buffers and indirect draws. Compute rasterization is a reported G1 capability, `compute_raster`, with its own capacity row in contract 13.3 from phase 2. The graphics popover names it.

**Section:** PLT Crash handling (Windows ARM64 row)
**Problem:** Until `crash-handler` supports Windows ARM64, PLT falls back to Windows Error Reporting local dumps. That feature needs administrator rights to configure under `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE`, which a per-user MSIX install does not have, and Microsoft documents that it does not support applications that do their own crash reporting.
**Evidence:** Microsoft: "Enabling the feature requires administrator privileges", configured under `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\Windows Error Reporting\LocalDumps`; "Applications that do their own custom crash reporting are not supported by this feature" (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/wer/collecting-user-mode-dumps). `crash-handling`'s target table marks `aarch64-pc-windows-msvc` unsupported (https://github.com/EmbarkStudios/crash-handling).
**Fix:** On Windows ARM64, each process installs an unhandled-exception filter that signals the existing crash-monitor process, and the monitor writes the minidump with `MiniDumpWriteDump`. PLT contributes this upstream in phase 0. WER local dumps remain only a documented administrator opt-in.

**Section:** PLT Release channels (D-PLT-27, D-PLT-21); PLT Open questions 10
**Problem:** D-PLT-27 says Crucible's 24-month LTS is "aligned with Wasmtime's LTS window". But Wasmtime supports each LTS for 24 months from its own release, and Crucible cuts its LTS from a 6-week stable train, so any delay between the two releases shortens upstream security support below Crucible's 24 months. Nothing fixes when in the year the Crucible LTS is cut.
**Evidence:** Wasmtime: "Each release that is a multiple of 12 is considered an LTS release and is supported for 24 months", released monthly on the 20th (https://docs.wasmtime.dev/stability-release.html). D-PLT-21: "moves between LTS releases only after the determinism suite passes". PLT open question 10: backports beyond the window need "a funded owner".
**Fix:** Answers PLT open question 10. Cut each Crucible LTS from the first stable train that follows a Wasmtime multiple-of-12 release and passes the suite, within 12 weeks. State the residual gap, at most 3 months, and fund backports for it. Regulated 10-year lines run their retired Wasmtime in sandboxed processes by default, with backports only when a customer contract funds a named owner. Record both rules in D-PLT-27.

**Section:** PLT Storage, hashing and updates
**Problem:** PLT gives Firefox's quota as "the smaller of 10% or 10 GiB", which is the best-effort limit. Because PLT requests persistence at first use, a granted origin gets up to 50% of disk. PLT also gives no quota for the iPadOS WKWebView shell, where embedded WebKit apps get about 15% of disk, not Safari's 60%.
**Evidence:** MDN: Firefox origins granted persistent storage "can store up to 50% of the total disk size, capped at 8 TiB"; for WebKit, "Other embedded WebKit apps get around 15% of total disk" (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Storage_API/Storage_quotas_and_eviction_criteria). PLT: "The engine requests persistence at first use".
**Fix:** The sentence reads "about 60% of disk in Chrome, Edge and Safari; in Firefox the smaller of 10% or 10 GiB, or up to 50% once persistence is granted; about 15% in embedded WebKit, which the iPadOS shell uses". The Tier 2 memory and storage plan uses the 15% figure.

**Section:** PLT Open questions 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 11 and 13
**Problem:** Seven PLT open questions remain undecided, although each can be decided now without blocking measurement.
**Evidence:** PLT Open questions 5 to 9, 11 and 13.
**Fix:** Decisions:
- **5, `detmath` speed:** correct rounding is never traded for speed; if `pow` or large-argument trigonometry misses its target, the target becomes 3 times glibc for that function, and the speed row files issues without blocking.
- **6, WGSL intervals:** GPU intervals stay `Preview`-only permanently; any `Interactive` use goes through the "GPU filters, CPU decides" role.
- **7, PE and Mach-O reproducibility:** if byte identity is unreachable after normalizing signatures and timestamps with a published tool, verification rests on SLSA provenance from two independent builders, stated per release.
- **8, chili:** no second scheduler before phase 4; it is revisited only if chili beats rayon by 1.3 times on two named kernels.
- **9, archive retention:** archived Wasm engine builds are kept for the longest supported line plus 2 years (12 years for regulated lines), signed by the TUF targets role and included in offline bundles; native builds are kept 5 years for LTS lines only.
- **11, fuel pricing:** `Usage` prices core-seconds, GPU-seconds and memory, never fuel; fuel stays a determinism and termination limit.
- **13, gateway app:** `apps/gateway` joins contract 12's crate map in the phase 2 ruling, with PLT packaging and `DeviceIo`.

**Section:** UIX Open questions 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9
**Problem:** Seven UIX open questions can be decided now, which removes undecided items from phase 1 and phase 2 planning.
**Evidence:** UIX Open questions 2 to 5 and 7 to 9.
**Fix:** Decisions:
- **2, mesh shaders:** no mesh shaders before phase 4, since WebGPU has none and they would add a G1-only path for a capacity gain alone.
- **3, Field evaluators:** FLX emits WGSL evaluators for H¹ Lagrange elements up to p = 4 on the immersed octree in phase 1; other discretizations use vertex samples with stated error until their evaluators exist.
- **4, web 64-bit atomics:** G2 compute rasterization waits until the feature ships in stable Chrome, Firefox and Safari; until then G2 uses the compacted index buffer.
- **5, 3D mouse SDK:** devices are read as HID on every desktop OS and through WebHID in Chromium, with the vendor driver as an optional path, so no SDK licence sits on a critical path; counsel still checks device terms.
- **7, usability thresholds:** 90% task success on core tasks gates each phase, and System Usability Scale scores are reported as a tracked metric, not a gate.
- **8, visionOS:** WebXR in Safari, since Safari 18.0 for visionOS 2 "adds support for immersive-vr sessions with WebXR" (https://webkit.org/blog/15865/webkit-features-in-safari-18-0/); a native shell only with a funded Tier 2 commitment.
- **9, saved views:** shared views live in the repository, and per-user views in a per-user store that creates no Changes.

**Section:** UIX Oracles (UIX-O-SNAP-2)
**Problem:** UIX-O-SNAP-2 judges 3D rendering against "references per backend" without saying where the references come from. If they are the renderer's own approved outputs, the oracle detects regressions, not errors, and an agent-built renderer can pass while wrong from the first reference.
**Evidence:** UIX-O-SNAP-2: "Mean ꟻLIP at most 0.01 against references per backend". UIX-O-OIT-1 and UIX-O-MAT-1, by contrast, name independent references (depth peeling, path tracing).
**Fix:** UIX-O-SNAP-2's references come from an independent CPU reference rasterizer kept in `oracles/uix/` and written separately from `apps/renderer`, for shading, edges and sections on the golden products. Regression images become a separate oracle.

**Section:** PLT and UIX [unverified] marks
**Problem:** Several [unverified] marks in PLT and UIX can be closed with primary sources. Leaving them open hides settled facts from implementers, as R6-47 found in round 1.
**Evidence:** See the Verified claims section: `Atomics.waitAsync` is Baseline 2025; tikv-jemallocator lists only Linux and macOS targets and gates its use on `not(target_env = "msvc")`; cargo-deny's four checks; cargo-auditable's embedded JSON; WER's local-dump configuration; Burns and Hunt 2013; WebXR on visionOS; the cross-origin isolation requirement for shared memory. The AWS-LC FIPS mark stays open: the aws-lc-rs README says AWS-LC-FIPS 3.x "has been submitted to NIST for certification" (https://github.com/aws/aws-lc-rs).
**Fix:** Remove these marks and cite the pages in the Verified claims section. Keep the AWS-LC mark and record the README's status, with a phase 2 check before FIPS mode ships.
